worked.title: Trace depends on the representation
steps: A cube quarter-turn has spatial eigenvalues $1,i,-i$, so its spatial trace is one. Its permutation on the four body diagonals is a four-cycle, so its diagonal permutation matrix has trace zero.
Characters are class functions because $\operatorname{tr}(ABA^{-1})=\operatorname{tr}(B)$. They remember traces of each group element, not just dimension at the identity.

practice.question: Give two one-dimensional representations of $C_2$ with different characters.
practice.hint: Send its generator to one or minus one.
practice.answer: The trivial and sign representations have rows $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$. Their dimensions agree, but their characters distinguish them.

title: Faithful and transitive ask different questions

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations
source.section: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.2 (24 rotations); Theorem 6.5 (Burnside). Full 48-element actions are original coordinate extensions.

intuition: Transitivity asks whether every position is reachable. Faithfulness asks whether every nonidentity symmetry can be detected somewhere. Neither condition forces the other.
explanation: The full cube group on its four diagonal lines is transitive but not faithful: central inversion fixes every line. Its action on the disjoint union of vertices and face centers is faithful but not transitive, because a symmetry preserves each of those two sets. The usual vertex action is both faithful and transitive. Thus reachability and detectability describe independent properties of an action.
proof: An element belongs to the kernel of the homomorphism into $S_X$ exactly when its induced permutation is the identity, which means fixing every point. This gives the intersection formula. The cube examples then establish the claimed distinctions: inversion witnesses a nontrivial diagonal kernel, and vertex faithfulness persists after adjoining a separate orbit of face centers.
pitfall: A transitive action need not be free. The rotation group is transitive on eight vertices but every vertex still has a three-element stabilizer.
prompt: For conjugation on S3, predict the kernel and the orbit of identity.
subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: The kernel is the center for conjugation; S3 has trivial center. One fixed point does not mean every group element acts trivially everywhere.
objective: Explain why a transitive action with a nontrivial stabilizer can still be faithful.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: Four action properties
steps: The natural $S_3$ action on three points is faithful and transitive, but not free because each point has a stabilizer of order two. The left regular action of $S_3$ on its six elements is free and transitive, hence regular.

The full cube group acting on vertices and faces together is faithful but not transitive: vertices never become faces. Its action on four diagonal lines is transitive but not faithful, since inversion fixes them all.

practice.question: Does a free action on a nonempty set have to be faithful? Does it have to be transitive?
practice.hint: A kernel element belongs to every stabilizer; free actions can have several orbits.
practice.answer: It is faithful because all stabilizers are trivial. It need not be transitive: two disjoint copies of a regular action give a free action with two orbits.

title: A stabilizer is local; a kernel is global

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations
source.section: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.2 (24 rotations); Theorem 6.5 (Burnside). Full 48-element actions are original coordinate extensions.

intuition: A stabilizer describes what one chosen object cannot detect. Intersecting stabilizers asks what the entire observation system cannot detect.
explanation: For a transitive action, choose $x$ and set $H=G_{x}$. The action is equivalent to left multiplication on $G/H$. A single stabilizer $H$ need not be normal: moving the chosen object conjugates its stabilizer. The kernel is the largest normal subgroup contained in $H$. In the rotation action on a face, $H$ has order 4 while the kernel is trivial.
theorem: H=G_x\Longrightarrow G/H\xrightarrow[\ gH\mapsto g\cdot x\ ]{\cong}G\cdot x\quad\text{as }G\text{-sets}
proof: The coset-to-orbit map is well-defined and bijective by the criterion $h^{-1}g\in H$. An element $a$ fixes every coset exactly when $agH=gH$ for all $g$, equivalently $g^{-1}ag\in H$. Intersect these conditions over $G$. Every normal subgroup contained in $H$ lies in all conjugates of $H$.
pitfall: A nontrivial stabilizer does not mean the action is unfaithful. Kernel elements must fix every object, rather than just the selected one.
prompt: Choose identity under conjugation; compare its stabilizer core with the action kernel.
subject: Groups & symmetry
labScope: For transitive actions the selected orbit is the whole set, so core and kernel agree. The distinction matters for nontransitive actions.
objective: Find a nontrivial stabilizer and a trivial kernel in the same action.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

worked.title: Intersect three stabilizers
steps: In the natural $S_3$ action, the stabilizers of points one, two and three are $\{e,(23)\}$, $\{e,(13)\}$ and $\{e,(12)\}$.

Each is nontrivial, but their intersection is only the identity. This intersection is the action kernel. In a transitive action, the stabilizers are conjugate, so the kernel is the core of any one of them.

practice.question: Why can a stabilizer change when the chosen point changes while the kernel stays the same?
practice.hint: One condition fixes one point; the other fixes the entire set.
practice.answer: Stabilizers impose point-specific equations. The kernel imposes all those equations at once, so it is independent of which point is selected for inspection.

title: Let a group act on itself in two ways

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples
source.section: §1.1, Definition 1.1; §1.3, geometric transformations. Coordinate examples developed here.

intuition: Left multiplication moves every group element uniformly. Conjugation instead changes the frame in which a symmetry is described, preserving its structural type.
explanation: The left regular action is faithful, free, and transitive: any group element can be moved to any other in exactly one way. In the conjugation action, orbits are conjugacy classes, the stabilizer of $x$ is its centralizer $C_G(x)$, and the kernel is the center Z(G). For cube rotations, conjugation carries a rotation axis to the transformed axis while preserving the rotation angle.
proof: For left multiplication, $gx=x$ implies $g=e$, and $yx^{-1}$ carries $x$ to $y$. For conjugation, $gxg^{-1}=x$ is equivalent to $gx=xg$, so the stabilizer is $C_G(x)$. Fixing every element means belonging to $Z(G)$. Orbit–stabilizer now gives $|\operatorname{Cl}(x)|=[G:C_G(x)]$.
pitfall: A left coset and a conjugacy class are different kinds of subsets. Conjugation is not generally transitive, and the identity always forms a singleton orbit.
prompt: Apply (12) to e under regular multiplication and under conjugation.

worked.title: Conjugation differs from translation
steps: In $D_4$, let r be a quarter-turn and s a reflection. Under conjugation by s, r becomes $srs^{-1}=r^{-1}$. Under left translation it becomes $sr$, a reflection.
Conjugation preserves element order, but left translation need not. The conjugacy orbit of r has two elements, while its regular-action orbit is the whole group.

practice.question: Which action fixes the identity under every acting element?
practice.hint: Compute both formulas at the identity.
practice.answer: Conjugation does: $geg^{-1}=e$. Left translation sends e to g, so only the identity acting element fixes it.

title: Count cube colorings by fixed colorings

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations
source.section: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.2 (24 rotations); Theorem 6.5 (Burnside). Full 48-element actions are original coordinate extensions.

intuition: Dividing the number of colorings by the group order fails when some colorings have extra symmetry. Burnside’s average automatically accounts for these smaller orbits.
explanation: Color the six faces independently from $k$ labeled colors, allowing repetition and allowing some colors to be unused. A coloring is fixed by a symmetry exactly when it is constant on each cycle of that symmetry’s face permutation. For rotations, the face cycle types and counts are $1^{6}$:1, $1^{2}2^{2}$:3, $1^{2}4$:6, $2^{3}$:6, and $3^{2}$:8. Including orientation reversal gives a different equivalence relation.
proof: Double-count the pairs $(g,c)$ with $g\cdot c=c$. Summing over $g$ gives the sum of fixed-coloring counts. Each orbit contributes $|G|$ pairs by orbit–stabilizer. A coloring fixed by a permutation is constant on each cycle, so a permutation with $r$ cycles fixes $k^r$ colorings. Summing the enumerated cycle types gives the displayed polynomials. Checks: $N_+(2)=N(2)=10$, while $N_+(3)=57$ and $N(3)=56$.
pitfall: These formulas do not require every color to appear. Prescribed color multiplicities need a different fixed-coloring count. Averaging only the 24 improper symmetries is not Burnside’s lemma because they are not a subgroup.
prompt: Open the coloring count and use three colors. Compare rotations-only with all symmetries: the face counts are 57 and 56. The lab counts orbits; it does not enumerate a representative of every coloring orbit.

title: Read the same motion through different cycles

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations
source.section: Chapter 6, Lemma 6.2 (24 rotations); Theorem 6.5 (Burnside). Full 48-element actions are original coordinate extensions.

intuition: One quarter turn is simultaneously a permutation of 8 vertices, 12 edges, 6 faces, and 4 diagonal lines. The cycle patterns expose different features of the same motion.
explanation: A face quarter turn has vertex cycle type $4^{2}$, edge type $4^{3}$, face type $1^{2}4$, and diagonal type 4. Its two fixed faces are obvious only in the face view, yet every view detects order four. Central inversion has order two on vertices, edges, and faces but acts identically on the four diagonal lines. An action can hide part or all of an element’s order.
proof: A permutation returns every point to its start exactly when the exponent is divisible by every cycle length, proving the least-common-multiple formula. Restrict $\varphi _X$ to the cyclic subgroup generated by $g$. Its kernel is the displayed intersection, so the first isomorphism theorem gives the order formula. In a faithful action the denominator is one, and every element’s order is preserved.
pitfall: A fixed face in a set action is a face preserved as a whole; its individual points may rotate. The order of an observed permutation equals the group-element order only when the restricted action detects all its powers.

title: Elimination reveals a permutation

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: Row operations simplify a matrix, but a permutation records the pivot pattern that triangular operations cannot erase.
definition: B=\{\text{invertible upper triangular matrices}\},\qquad W=\{\text{permutation matrices}\}.
explanation: Work in $G=\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$ over a field. Left multiplication performs row operations; right multiplication performs column operations. Allowing only upper triangular operations leaves a unique relative position, indexed by a permutation. These relative positions are the double cosets of $B$. This is the matrix version of comparing two complete flags.
proof: Upper triangular row operations isolate a last nonzero pivot in each successive column. A permutation puts the pivots in standard positions; triangular column operations remove the remaining entries. For uniqueness, triangular transformations preserve the ranks of the appropriate flag intersections, which determine the permutation. This also shows that invertible diagonal matrices and transvections generate the general linear group.
pitfall: The permutation is unique; the two triangular factors usually are not. A double coset is not a quotient group.
prompt: In dimension $2$, compare an upper triangular matrix with one whose lower-left entry is nonzero. They lie in the two different cells.

worked.title: Two cells in dimension two
steps: The identity cell is $B$. The other cell corresponds to the swap matrix and has $q|B|=36$ elements.
The two cells partition $G$: $12+36=48$. Triangular reduction never changes which cell contains the matrix.

reading.title: Counting bases and using elementary matrices
paragraphs: An elementary abelian group of order $p^n$ is an $n$-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb F_p$, so its automorphisms form $\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F_p)$. Choosing independent columns in order gives $|\operatorname{GL}_n(q)|=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(q^n-q^i)$.

The transvection $X_{ij}(a)=I+aE_{ij}$ adds $a$ times row $j$ to row $i$ under left multiplication. It has determinant one, satisfies $X_{ij}(a)X_{ij}(b)=X_{ij}(a+b)$, and is conjugated by a permutation matrix by relabelling its indices. For distinct indices, the convention $[x,y]=xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$ gives $[X_{ij}(a),X_{jk}(b)]=X_{ik}(ab)$.

Elimination reduces an invertible matrix using transvections and invertible diagonal matrices. These generate the general linear group. Restricting which row operations are allowed preserves information about relative flags and exposes the Bruhat permutation.

source.title: Alperin & Bell · Groups and Representations

reading.title: Existence and uniqueness of the Bruhat cell
paragraphs: Let $B$ be the invertible upper triangular matrices and $W$ the permutation matrices. Then $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}BwB$. Triangular row and column operations yield existence; ranks of intersections between the standard flag and its image determine the permutation uniquely.

For $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ invertible, $c=0$ places the matrix in $B$, while $c\ne0$ places it in the other cell $BsB$. The lower-left entry is the first nontrivial relative-flag invariant. There are two cells, although either cell contains many matrices.

title: Remove the scalar symmetries

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: A scalar matrix moves every vector but fixes every line. Projectivising removes exactly that invisible motion.
explanation: For $n\ge2$, the center of $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$ consists of nonzero scalar matrices; in $\operatorname{SL}_n(F)$ they also satisfy $\lambda^n=1$. The action on one-dimensional subspaces factors through the projective quotient. Transvections generate the special linear group, and outside two small exceptions they are commutators.
proof: The determinant gives the first division by $q-1$; the scalar center gives the second. For simplicity, use the faithful primitive action on projective points, the abelian group of transvections with a fixed image line, normal in its stabilizer, and generation by its conjugates. A nontrivial normal subgroup must be transitive; the quotient becomes abelian, whereas the special linear group is perfect outside the exceptions. Hence the quotient is trivial.
pitfall: Simplicity is a statement about the projective quotient. The special linear group can have a nontrivial scalar center. At the exceptions, $\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb F_2)\cong S_3$ and $\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb F_3)\cong A_4$.
prompt: Follow the two quotients: determinant first, scalar center second.

worked.title: A simple group of order sixty
steps: The special linear subgroup has order $480/4=120$. Its center is $\{I,-I\}$.
The projective quotient has order $60$ and is simple. It is isomorphic to $A_5$.

reading.title: Determinants, scalar centers and simplicity
paragraphs: The determinant is onto $F^\times$ with kernel $\operatorname{SL}_n(F)$. Over $\mathbb F_q$, divide the general linear group order by $q-1$. Commuting with every elementary matrix forces a central matrix to be scalar. In the special linear group its scalar satisfies $\lambda^n=1$.

Transvections generate the special linear group. Outside $n=2$ over the fields of orders two and three, they are commutators, so this group is perfect. Its action on projective points is doubly transitive; the kernel is its scalar center. Combining primitivity and conjugate root subgroups proves simplicity of $\operatorname{PSL}_n(F)$ with precisely those two exceptions.

For $n=2$, the order is $q(q^2-1)/\gcd(2,q-1)$. Thus the two exceptional projective groups are $S_3$ and $A_4$, whereas $\operatorname{PSL}_2(4)$ and $\operatorname{PSL}_2(5)$ are both isomorphic to $A_5$.

title: Blocks detect hidden quotients of an action

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: An action can look transitive on points yet move larger packets intact. A block is one such packet.
definition: \Delta\subseteq X\text{ a block}\iff\Delta\ne\varnothing,\quad g\Delta=\Delta\text{ or }g\Delta\cap\Delta=\varnothing\quad(\forall g\in G).
explanation: Assume $X$ is a transitive $G$-set with $|X|\ge2$ and fix $x\in X$. Blocks containing $x$ correspond to subgroups between $G_x$ and $G$: a subgroup $H$ gives $Hx$. The trivial blocks are singletons and $X$. An action is primitive when no other blocks exist. Double transitivity means transitivity on ordered pairs of distinct points.
theorem: G\curvearrowright X\text{ transitive},\ |X|\ge2:\quad X\text{ primitive}\iff G_x\text{ proper maximal in }G;\qquad\text{doubly transitive}\Rightarrow\text{primitive}
proof: For a block $\Delta$ containing $x$, its setwise stabilizer $H$ contains $G_x$: a translate by an element fixing x meets $\Delta$, hence equals it. Transitivity lets every y in $\Delta$ be written gx; that translate also meets $\Delta$, so g belongs to H and $\Delta=Hx$. Conversely take $G_x\le H\le G$. If $gHx$ meets $Hx$, write $gh_1x=h_2x$; then $h_2^{-1}gh_1\in G_x\le H$, so $g\in H$ and $gHx=Hx$. Thus Hx is a block, and its setwise stabilizer is H by the same argument. The trivial blocks correspond to $G_x$ and G. For degree at least two, having no intermediate blocks is therefore equivalent to $G_x$ being proper maximal. In a doubly transitive action, if a block contains distinct x,y, the stabilizer of x sends y to every other point while preserving the block, so the block is all of X.
pitfall: Primitive does not mean regular or faithful. A prime-degree transitive action is primitive, but need not be doubly transitive. We exclude degree one: its point stabilizer is the whole group, not a proper maximal subgroup.
prompt: Compare the square action with the triangle action. Opposite pairs form blocks for the square.

worked.title: Opposite vertices of a square
steps: For $D_4$ acting on four vertices, $\Delta=\{0,2\}$ is a block.
Every symmetry either preserves $\Delta$ or sends it to $\{1,3\}$.
The action is transitive but imprimitive. The intermediate subgroup has order $4$, between a vertex stabilizer of order $2$ and $D_4$ of order $8$.
For a singleton action X={x}, the only nonempty block is X itself, so there is no nontrivial block; nevertheless Gₓ=G is not a proper maximal subgroup. This is why |X|≥2 is indispensable.
For the square, the setwise stabilizer H of {0,2} has G₀<H<D₄. The block–subgroup correspondence gives a concrete witness to imprimitivity.

reading.title: Blocks, maximal stabilizers and double cosets
paragraphs: For a transitive action, a block containing $x$ is $Hx$ for a unique intermediate subgroup $G_x\le H\le G$. Thus primitivity is equivalent to maximality of the stabilizer. Double transitivity implies primitivity, since a block containing two points must contain every point.

Counting the fibers of $(h,k)\mapsto hxk$ gives $|HxK|=|H||K|/|H\cap xKx^{-1}|$. Under conjugation, element and subgroup stabilizers are respectively centralizers and normalizers. Hence $|g^G|=[G:C_G(g)]$ and the number of conjugates of $H$ is $[G:N_G(H)]$.

title: Coprime normal structure splits

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: A normal subgroup can obstruct splitting. Coprime size and index remove that obstruction.
definition: N\trianglelefteq G,\quad \gcd(|N|,[G:N])=1;\qquad H\text{ complements }N\iff G=NH,\ N\cap H=1.
explanation: For a finite group, a Hall subgroup has order coprime to its index. Schur–Zassenhaus says that a normal Hall subgroup has a complement, so the group is a semidirect product. Existence of a complement and conjugacy of complements are separate assertions; the latter has an elementary treatment when the normal subgroup or quotient is solvable.
theorem: G\text{ finite},\ N\trianglelefteq G\text{ Hall}\Longrightarrow G\cong N\rtimes H\text{ for some complement }|H|=[G:N]
proof: Induct on $|G|$. The Frattini argument reduces to a smaller normalizer unless a chosen Sylow subgroup of $N$ is normal in $G$. Continue reducing to an abelian normal subgroup. Its extension defect is a $2$-cocycle; averaging over the quotient annihilates the defect because the quotient order is invertible on the abelian Hall subgroup. A corrected section is a homomorphism and yields the complement.
pitfall: Normality is essential to this splitting statement. A semidirect product need not be direct, and without coprimality a complement can fail to exist.
prompt: Compare the normal subgroup of order three in the triangle group with the subgroup of order two in the cyclic group of order four.

worked.title: Split and non-split extensions
steps: $S_3=C_3\rtimes C_2$: a transposition supplies a complement to the normal subgroup $A_3$.
In $C_4$, the subgroup $C_2$ is normal but its order and index are not coprime.
The unique subgroup of order $2$ is the kernel itself, so it cannot be a complement. The extension of $C_2$ by $C_2$ does not split.

reading.title: Why a coprime normal subgroup splits
paragraphs: A Hall subgroup has order coprime to its index. Schur–Zassenhaus gives a complement to every normal Hall subgroup of a finite group. Thus $G=NH$, $N\cap H=1$ and $G\cong N\rtimes H$. Conjugacy of complements is obtained under the source’s solvability hypothesis on one of the two factors.

The coprimality is essential: the subgroup of order two in $C_4$ has no complement. For an abelian normal subgroup, averaging with the inverse of the coprime index removes the factor-set obstruction; induction reduces the general existence argument to this mechanism.

title: A section remembers the failure to split

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Maps & quotients
intuition: Choose one representative in each quotient class. Their products need not equal the representative of the product; the discrepancy is useful data.
explanation: A section is initially only a set map. Conjugation by $t(a)$ gives $\varphi(a)\in\operatorname{Aut}(N)$. Associativity imposes compatibility between $\varphi$ and $f$. If $N=A$ is abelian, the action is a genuine homomorphism and the defect is an additive $2$-cocycle. Replacing the section changes the cocycle by a coboundary.
theorem: A\text{ abelian with fixed }H\text{-action}:\quad a\cdot f(b,c)-f(ab,c)+f(a,bc)-f(a,b)=0;\quad H^2(H,A)=Z^2(H,A)/B^2(H,A)
proof: Expand $t(a)t(b)t(c)$ in its two associations to derive the cocycle identity. Under $t^{\prime}(a)=c(a)t(a)$, calculate the new defect: $f^{\prime}(a,b)=f(a,b)+c(a)+a\cdot c(b)-c(ab)$. Thus a class is zero exactly when a representative section can be corrected to a homomorphism. For nonabelian kernels, retain the full factor pair; the induced map to $\operatorname{Out}(N)$ is independent of the section.
pitfall: Equivalent extensions must respect the specified kernel and quotient maps. Isomorphic middle groups can define inequivalent extensions. A factor pair need not give an action into $\operatorname{Aut}(N)$ without an inner-automorphism correction.
prompt: Use carries in addition modulo four as the defect for a section of its quotient modulo two.

worked.title: A carry is a cocycle
steps: Write elements of $C_4$ as $2u+a$, where $u,a\in\{0,1\}$.
Addition is $(u,a)+(v,b)=(u+v+\lfloor(a+b)/2\rfloor,\ a+b\bmod2)$, with the first coordinate also modulo $2$.
The carry $f(1,1)=1$ obstructs a homomorphic section. Deleting the carry gives $C_2\times C_2$, a different extension.

reading.title: Factor sets, cohomology and changing a section
paragraphs: Fix an action of $H$ on an abelian group $A$, written additively. A normalized section of an extension gives multiplication $(a,x)(b,y)=(a+x\cdot b+f(x,y),xy)$. Associativity is exactly $x\cdot f(y,z)-f(xy,z)+f(x,yz)-f(x,y)=0$.

Changing the section by $t:H\to A$ replaces $f$ by $f+\delta t$, where $\delta t(x,y)=t(x)+x\cdot t(y)-t(xy)$. Thus $H^2(H,A)$ classifies extensions with fixed action and fixed identifications of kernel and quotient. The zero class is the split extension.

Within a split extension, complements correspond to crossed homomorphisms $d(xy)=d(x)+x\cdot d(y)$. Conjugating by $A$ changes a crossed homomorphism by a principal one, giving the $H^1$ description. These equivalence relations are part of the classification, not optional notation.

title: Peel away commutators

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: One commutator subgroup removes the abelian information. Solvability means that repeating this process eventually leaves nothing.
definition: G^{(0)}=G,\qquad G^{(i+1)}=[G^{(i)},G^{(i)}],\qquad G\text{ solvable}\iff G^{(r)}=1\text{ for some }r.
explanation: Solvability is equivalent to admitting a finite subnormal series with abelian factors. It passes to subgroups and quotients, and if both a normal subgroup and its quotient are solvable, so is the whole group. For finite groups it is equivalent to having only prime-order composition factors, or elementary abelian chief factors.
theorem: G\text{ finite solvable},\ |G|=mn,\ \gcd(m,n)=1:\quad\text{Hall subgroups of order }m\text{ exist and are conjugate};\quad\text{each subgroup with prime divisors among those of }m\text{ lies in some such Hall subgroup}
proof: For the derived-series criterion, each abelian factor forces the next commutator subgroup into the next term. Closure under extensions follows by first descending into the solvable kernel and then through its derived series. For Hall existence and conjugacy, induct using a minimal normal subgroup: in a solvable group it is elementary abelian. Pass to the quotient, then lift and use coprime splitting or the corresponding elementary induction.
pitfall: Solvable is weaker than nilpotent. The factors in a solvable series are abelian; the whole group need not be. Hall existence for every coprime divisor characterises finite solvable groups, but one Hall subgroup alone does not.
prompt: Follow the derived series of the symmetric group on four points; compare with the group on three points.

worked.title: Three steps for the symmetric group
steps: $[S_4,S_4]=A_4$: the sign map gives an abelian quotient, and commutators generate the three-cycles.
The three abelian successive quotients show that $S_4$ has derived length $3$. It is not nilpotent because its Sylow subgroups are not all normal.

reading.title: Equivalent series, Hall subgroups and affine actions
paragraphs: Solvability is equivalent to a normal or subnormal series with abelian factors. It passes to subgroups and quotients and is closed under extensions and finite direct products. For a group with a composition series, it means every composition factor has prime order; equivalently its chief factors are elementary abelian.

A finite solvable group has Hall subgroups for every selection of primes. Such Hall subgroups are conjugate, and every subgroup using only those primes lies in one. Conversely existence of Hall subgroups for all prime selections characterizes finite solvability.

A faithful finite solvable primitive permutation group has a regular elementary abelian minimal normal subgroup. Identify the points with that vector space: translations give the normal subgroup and the point stabilizer acts linearly. This places the group inside an affine general linear group.

Burnside’s two-prime theorem is proved using characters later. The odd-order theorem says every finite group of odd order is solvable; its proof lies far beyond these notes. A further criterion detects nonsolvability through nonidentity elements of pairwise coprime orders satisfying $xy=z$; it is a structural theorem, not an efficient search algorithm.

title: Central layers control the whole group

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: A central series lets you remove one layer at a time, with each layer commuting with everything that remains.
explanation: A group is nilpotent exactly when its lower central series reaches $1$, or its upper central series reaches $G$, in finitely many steps. For finite groups this is also equivalent to every Sylow subgroup being normal, to being the direct product of the Sylow subgroups, and to every proper subgroup being properly contained in its normalizer.
theorem: G\text{ finite nilpotent}\iff G\cong\prod_{p\mid |G|}P_p;\qquad P/\Phi(P)\cong\mathbb F_p^d\quad(P\text{ a finite }p\text{-group}).
proof: A nontrivial finite $p$-group has nontrivial center by the class equation. Apply the argument repeatedly to central quotients. For a finite nilpotent group, the normalizer condition forces Sylow normalizers to be the whole group. Conversely normal Sylow subgroups of coprime orders commute and form a direct product. For the Frattini quotient, maximal subgroups of a $p$-group have index $p$, so all commutators and $p$th powers lie in their intersection.
pitfall: Derived and central series are different. Every nilpotent group is solvable, but $S_3$ is solvable and not nilpotent. Finite nilpotent groups need not be abelian.
prompt: For the quaternion group, identify its center and its quotient. Compare with the dihedral group of order eight.

worked.title: A nonabelian group of class two
steps: In $Q_8$, commutators lie in $\{\pm1\}$, which is central.
Thus $\gamma_2(Q_8)=\{\pm1\}$ and $\gamma_3(Q_8)=1$.
The upper series is $1<\{\pm1\}<Q_8$. Both central series have length $2$.

reading.title: Central series and the finite nilpotence tests
paragraphs: The lower central series is $\gamma_1(G)=G$, $\gamma_{i+1}(G)=[\gamma_i(G),G]$. The upper central series starts at $1$ and pulls back the centers of successive quotients. Termination of the first at $1$ is equivalent to the second reaching $G$. Nilpotent groups are solvable.

For a finite group, nilpotence is equivalent to all Sylow subgroups being normal, to their internal direct product, to all maximal subgroups being normal, and to every proper subgroup being properly contained in its normalizer. Finiteness matters: these are not unrestricted equivalences.

The product of finite normal nilpotent subgroups is nilpotent; their product is the Fitting subgroup. In a finite solvable group it is an important source of normal structure. In $S_3$ the Fitting subgroup is $C_3$, while the whole group is solvable but not nilpotent.

title: Bilinear rules become linear maps

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Modules & representations
intuition: A tensor product packages every bilinear calculation into one linear object. Pure tensors are building blocks, not every possible tensor.
definition: (u+u^{\prime})\otimes v=u\otimes v+u^{\prime}\otimes v,\quad u\otimes(v+v^{\prime})=u\otimes v+u\otimes v^{\prime},\quad (ur)\otimes v=u\otimes(rv).
explanation: For a right $R$-module $U$ and a left $R$-module $V$, the tensor product is generated by symbols $u\otimes v$ subject to additivity and the balancing relation. Over a field, bases give a product basis. For finite-dimensional $U$, a dual vector and a vector define the rank-one map $u\mapsto\varphi(u)v$. Precisely, every additive-in-each-variable map $b:U\times V\to A$ to an abelian group with $b(ur,v)=b(u,rv)$ factors uniquely through an additive map $U\otimes_R V\to A$. Over a noncommutative ring this tensor product is an abelian group; an additional scalar action requires additional structure.
theorem: U,V\text{ finite-dimensional }F\text{-spaces}:\quad U^*\otimes_F V\cong\operatorname{Hom}_F(U,V),\quad\varphi\otimes v\mapsto[u\mapsto\varphi(u)v];\quad\dim(U\otimes_F V)=\dim U\dim V
proof: Choose a basis $e_i$ of $U$ with dual basis $e_i^*$. The tensors $e_i^*\otimes f_j$ map to the matrix units, so the displayed map is bijective. Its formula is independent of the chosen bases. For group modules, use $g\varphi=\varphi\circ g^{-1}$ and $g(\varphi\otimes v)=g\varphi\otimes gv$; evaluation then proves equivariance.
pitfall: The balancing relation requires the correct left/right module sides. A general tensor is a sum of pure tensors; for example a rank-two matrix is not one outer product.
prompt: Choose cyclic right/left ℤ-modules, scalar and vectors; predict gcd generator order and both balanced expressions.

worked.title: Tensor two cyclic modules
steps: The tensor product $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z$ is generated by $t=[1]\otimes[1]$.
Balancing and additivity give $2t=0$ and $3t=0$. Subtracting gives $t=3t-2t=0$, so the entire tensor product is zero.
In contrast, $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\otimes\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\cong\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$: the balanced map $([a],[b])\mapsto[ab]$ sends $t$ to a nonzero class and every tensor is a multiple of $t$.

reading.title: Balancing, direct sums and equivariance
paragraphs: The maps $r\otimes m\mapsto rm$ and $m\mapsto1\otimes m$ show $R\otimes_R M\cong M$. Tensor products distribute over direct sums because the same balanced bilinear map can be specified separately on each summand.

For finite-dimensional $U$, $U^*\otimes_F V\cong\operatorname{Hom}_F(U,V)$ via $\varphi\otimes v\mapsto[u\mapsto\varphi(u)v]$. For group representations, use the contragredient action on the dual and conjugation on Hom; the map is then equivariant.

A linear group action extends uniquely by linearity to a group-algebra module. If the group is finite, finite generation over the group algebra is equivalent to finite vector-space dimension, since the algebra itself has a finite basis indexed by group elements.

title: An algebra splits into matrix blocks

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Modules & representations
intuition: A semisimple algebra looks complicated until its simple modules reveal independent matrix blocks.
definition: M\text{ semisimple}\iff M=\bigoplus_i S_i\text{ with each }S_i\text{ simple}.
explanation: Here all algebras are finite-dimensional over a field and have an identity, and modules are finite-dimensional and unital. A module is semisimple exactly when each submodule has a complement. An algebra is semisimple exactly when its regular left module is semisimple. Matrix blocks classify the resulting algebra, while multiplicities classify its modules.
theorem: A\text{ finite-dimensional unital over }F:\quad A\text{ semisimple}\iff A\cong\prod_i M_{n_i}(D_i),\quad D_i\text{ finite-dimensional division }F\text{-algebras}
proof: Decompose the regular module into isotypic pieces $n_iS_i$. Schur gives zero homomorphisms between nonisomorphic simple modules and division rings of endomorphisms on each simple. Thus its endomorphism ring is a product of matrix rings. Right multiplication identifies $A^{\mathrm{op}}$ with $\operatorname{End}_A(A)$; taking opposite rings recovers the claimed decomposition. Over an algebraically closed field, the division algebras are the field itself.
pitfall: Semisimple does not mean commutative. A simple algebra may have many proper left ideals: simplicity excludes proper nonzero two-sided ideals. The finite-dimensional hypothesis matters.
prompt: Choose M2(F), T2(F) or F[C2], a coefficient field and matrix units; predict radical, quotient blocks and splitting before revealing.

worked.title: The group algebra of the triangle group
steps: Over $\mathbb C$, $S_3$ has irreducible degrees $1,1,2$.
Hence $\mathbb C S_3\cong\mathbb C\times\mathbb C\times M_2(\mathbb C)$ and its dimension is $1^2+1^2+2^2=6$.
There are $2^3=8$ two-sided ideals, one for each choice of whole blocks. The regular module contains the two-dimensional simple twice.

reading.title: From complements to matrix blocks
paragraphs: Throughout this discussion algebras and modules are finite-dimensional over a field. A module is semisimple exactly when every submodule is a direct summand. Submodules and quotients remain semisimple. A unital algebra is semisimple exactly when its regular module is semisimple.

Choose representatives $S_i$ of the simple modules. Schur’s lemma makes $\operatorname{End}_A(S_i)$ a division algebra and kills Hom between different representatives. On $\bigoplus_i n_iS_i$, endomorphisms consequently form a product of matrix algebras. Right multiplication gives $\operatorname{End}_A(A)\cong A^{\mathrm{op}}$, which accounts for the opposite-ring convention in the proof.

The natural column module is the only simple module of $M_n(D)$ up to isomorphism, and its regular module consists of $n$ copies. Matrix units show every nonzero two-sided ideal is the whole matrix algebra. Ideals in a product split by factors, so a semisimple algebra has exactly the ideals obtained by selecting whole simple blocks.

Over an algebraically closed field, a finite-dimensional division algebra is the field itself: every element has an eigenvalue, and its difference from that scalar cannot be invertible. Thus the blocks are ordinary matrix algebras over the ground field.

title: The radical is what simple modules cannot see

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Modules & representations
intuition: The radical collects the obstruction to semisimplicity. Removing it leaves exactly the matrix blocks seen by simple modules.
explanation: For a finite-dimensional unital algebra, the Jacobson radical is nilpotent, is the largest nilpotent two-sided ideal, and is the smallest left submodule of the regular module with semisimple quotient. The quotient $A/J(A)$ is semisimple and has the same simple modules as $A$. These descriptions fit the commutative radical picture into noncommutative representation theory.
proof: A nilpotent ideal annihilates every simple module: otherwise its image is the whole module, and iteration contradicts nilpotence. Intersecting annihilators therefore contains all nilpotent ideals. Finite length and the semisimple quotient show this intersection is itself nilpotent. For a module, pass to the quotient by $J(A)M$ and use the semisimplicity of $A/J(A)$; the socle is the part already annihilated by the radical.
pitfall: The radical is nilpotent here because the algebra is finite-dimensional. For a general commutative ring the nilradical need not be nilpotent. Nilpotent elements need not individually form an ideal in a noncommutative algebra.
prompt: Choose M2(F), T2(F) or F[C2], a coefficient field and matrix units; predict radical, quotient blocks and splitting before revealing.

worked.title: Upper triangular matrices
steps: For $T_2(F)$, the strictly upper triangular matrices form an ideal $J$ with $J^2=0$.
The diagonal map has kernel $J$ and image $F\times F$. Thus $T_2(F)/J\cong F\times F$.
On the natural column module, the socle is the first coordinate line; the quotient is the other one-dimensional simple. The module is not the direct sum of those lines as a $T_2(F)$-module.

reading.title: The radical, unitisation and common fixed vectors
paragraphs: In finite dimension, sums of nilpotent two-sided ideals are nilpotent: sufficiently long products must contain enough factors from one ideal. This gives a largest nilpotent ideal. Intersections of submodules with semisimple quotients again have semisimple quotient, yielding a smallest such submodule.

For a unital algebra these constructions equal the common annihilator of simple modules, namely $J(A)$. Hence $A/J(A)$ is semisimple and $A$ is semisimple exactly when it has no nonzero nilpotent ideals.

An algebra without identity embeds as an ideal in $F\oplus A$, with multiplication $(r,a)(s,b)=(rs,rb+sa+ab)$. A nonzero finite-dimensional algebra without nonzero nilpotent ideals acquires its own identity through its semisimple block decomposition.

The source’s nilpotent-span theorem and its application to the algebra generated by differences $h-I$ provide a common fixed nonzero vector for a unipotent matrix group. Inducting on the quotient then yields simultaneous upper unitriangular form. “Every generator is nilpotent” by itself is insufficient: the associative algebra they generate need not be nilpotent.

reading.title: Module layers and matrix-ring modules
paragraphs: For a finite-dimensional unital algebra, $\operatorname{rad}M=J(A)M$ and $\operatorname{soc}M=\{m:J(A)m=0\}$. Iterating gives radical and socle filtrations. The successive layers are semisimple, but the full module may glue them in a nontrivial way.

Matrix units identify modules over $M_n(A)$ with modules over $A$: take $e_{11}M$ in one direction and column vectors in the other. This explains why matrix rings share simple-module structure with the coefficient algebra even though their vector-space dimensions differ. Free and projective modules should not be confused with simple modules.

title: Character values are algebraic integers

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Modules & representations
intuition: Traces are sums of roots of unity. That arithmetic information forces divisibility that linear algebra alone does not reveal.
definition: \alpha\text{ algebraic integer}\iff f(\alpha)=0\text{ for some monic }f\in\mathbb Z[X].
explanation: Algebraic integers form a ring, and a rational algebraic integer is an ordinary integer. Since a finite-order complex matrix has roots of unity as eigenvalues, every character value is an algebraic integer. For an irreducible character, the scalar by which a conjugacy-class sum acts is also an algebraic integer.
theorem: G\text{ finite},\quad\chi\in\operatorname{Irr}_{\mathbb C}(G):\quad \frac{|g^G|\chi(g)}{\chi(1)}\text{ is an algebraic integer};\qquad\chi(1)\mid|G|.
proof: Class sums multiply with integer structure constants in the center of $\mathbb CG$. Their scalar actions satisfy monic integer polynomials, by the characteristic polynomial of this multiplication. Row orthogonality expresses $|G|/\chi(1)$ as a sum of products of these algebraic integers with conjugate character values. It is rational, so it is an integer.
pitfall: Character values need not be rational or integral as ordinary numbers. Divisibility concerns the degree of a complex irreducible character, not an arbitrary representation dimension.
prompt: Compare degrees with the group order, then compare ordinary integer character values with the golden-ratio values in the alternating group of degree five.

worked.title: The degree test
steps: The irreducible degrees of $A_5$ are $1,3,3,4,5$. Each divides $60$.
The three-dimensional characters take $(1+\sqrt5)/2$ and $(1-\sqrt5)/2$ on the five-cycle classes.
These values are not integers, but both satisfy the monic polynomial $X^2-X-1$.

reading.title: The arithmetic behind character divisibility
paragraphs: A rational root of a monic integer polynomial has denominator one. Algebraic integers form a ring: finitely many generators lie in a finitely generated integer module stable under multiplication, and the determinant argument gives a monic equation for any sum or product.

Character values are sums of roots of unity. Class sums multiply with integer coefficients; their scalar actions on irreducibles therefore satisfy monic integer equations. Row orthogonality then expresses $|G|/\chi(1)$ as an algebraic integer. Since it is rational, it is an integer.

If a normalized nonzero character value is an algebraic integer, all its Galois conjugates have absolute value at most one. Its nonzero integer norm forces equality everywhere. This is the arithmetic step that turns a nonzero normalized trace into a scalar action.

title: A small conjugacy class forces normal structure

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: A group whose order uses only two primes cannot hide a nonabelian simple factor. Character arithmetic explains why.
explanation: Burnside proves that every finite group of order $p^aq^b$ is solvable. The key character-theoretic obstruction says that a nonabelian finite simple group has no conjugacy class of size a nontrivial prime power. Prime-power here describes the size of the class, not the order of its representative. In the nonabelian simple case, $z$ is not central in $G$, so the class size is greater than one. Having excluded all nonabelian simple groups of two-prime order, induction on group order makes both a proper normal subgroup and its quotient solvable; their extension is solvable.
proof: This is a roadmap, not a proof of the character-theoretic lemma. Import the theorem that a nonabelian finite simple group has no nontrivial prime-power conjugacy class. For a hypothetical nonabelian simple group of order $p^aq^b$ with both primes present, choose $1\ne z\in Z(Q)$ for a Sylow $q$-subgroup $Q$. Since $Q\le C_G(z)$, its class size is a power of $p$; simplicity forces $Z(G)=1$, so that size is greater than one, contradicting the imported theorem. Prime-power groups are excluded by their nontrivial centers. Now induct on group order: every proper nontrivial normal subgroup and its quotient have orders involving at most the same two primes, hence are solvable; extensions of solvable groups are solvable. The scalar preimage $\{g:\rho(g)\text{ is scalar}\}$ used in proofs of the imported lemma is not the ordinary kernel $\{g:\rho(g)=I\}$.
pitfall: Do not confuse this theorem with the orbit-counting lemma also named after Burnside. A group of prime-power order has nontrivial center; the class-size argument addresses the two-prime case.
prompt: Predict the class size of a nonidentity element central in a Sylow subgroup before checking the centralizer index.

worked.title: Why order thirty-six is solvable
steps: $36=2^2\cdot3^2$. Every simple composition factor has order involving at most the primes $2$ and $3$.
The class-size obstruction excludes any nonabelian simple factor of that order type.
Every simple factor therefore has prime order. This is the composition-factor criterion for solvability.

reading.title: Prime-power class sizes and counting commutators
paragraphs: For a conjugacy class of nontrivial prime-power size, combine a Bézout relation for an irreducible degree coprime to that prime with integrality of the central scalar. The normalized nonzero character value must have absolute value one, so the element acts as a scalar. Orthogonality ensures a suitable nontrivial irreducible exists; simplicity then fails.

If a nonabelian simple group had order $p^aq^b$, take a nonidentity central element of a Sylow $q$-subgroup. Its centralizer contains that Sylow subgroup, making its conjugacy class a nontrivial power of $p$. The obstruction rules this out, and induction over normal subgroups proves solvability.

Character methods also count solutions of commutator equations. For the convention $[x,y]=xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$, the number of pairs with $[x,y]=g$ is $|G|\sum_{\chi\in\operatorname{Irr}(G)}\chi(g)/\chi(1)$. At the identity this becomes $|G|$ times the number of conjugacy classes, agreeing with direct counting of commuting pairs.

practice.answer: A nonidentity central element generates a nontrivial central normal subgroup. A nonabelian simple group has trivial center, so the chosen nonidentity z cannot have a singleton class.

title: Fixed-point-free motions form a subgroup

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory

subject: Groups & symmetry
intuition: If no nonidentity motion fixes two points, the motions fixing no point assemble into a normal subgroup after adding the identity.
explanation: For a finite faithful permutation group satisfying this condition, the identity together with the fixed-point-free elements is the Frobenius kernel. It is a regular normal subgroup. A point stabilizer is a complement, so the group is a semidirect product. The closure assertion is the surprising part: it does not follow just by inspecting fixed points of a product.
theorem: G\text{ finite, action faithful transitive},\ |X|>1,\ |\operatorname{Fix}_X(g)|\le1\ (g\ne1):\quad N=\{1\}\cup\{g:\operatorname{Fix}_X(g)=\varnothing\}\trianglelefteq G,\quad G=N\rtimes G_x
proof: Let the point stabilizer be $H$. Distinct conjugates intersect trivially, so induction of nontrivial characters of $H$ has tightly controlled inner products. Frobenius reciprocity constructs a character whose kernel is exactly the claimed set. This proves closure and normality; the count then shows $|N|=|X|$, giving regularity and the complement.
pitfall: The fixed-point condition must hold for every nonidentity group element. A merely transitive action need not have such a kernel. The word “Frobenius” here names a permutation-group theorem, distinct from reciprocity.
prompt: Consider affine transformations of a finite prime field. Nonidentity translations fix no point; a nontranslation fixes exactly one.

worked.title: Affine motions of five points
steps: Let $G=\{x\mapsto ax+b:a\in\mathbb F_5^\times,b\in\mathbb F_5\}$, of order $20$.
For $a=1,b\ne0$, there is no fixed point. For $a\ne1$, the unique fixed point is $x=b/(1-a)$.
The translations form the normal kernel $C_5$, and maps fixing zero form a complement $C_4$.

reading.title: The Frobenius kernel and its character-theoretic proof
paragraphs: In a finite faithful transitive action with more than one point, assume no nonidentity element fixes two points. Point stabilizers intersect trivially. Counting their conjugates shows that the identity together with the fixed-point-free elements has exactly as many elements as the set being acted on.

Counting does not show closure. Frobenius’s theorem supplies that missing step using induced characters and orthogonality: the set is a normal subgroup, acting regularly. A point stabilizer is a complement. In the affine action of $\mathbb F_q\rtimes\mathbb F_q^\times$, the kernel consists of translations.

practice.question: Where does x→2x+1 fix a point in F₅?
practice.hint: Identify the objects and the hypothesis needed before calculating.
practice.answer: (1−2)x=1 gives −x=1, hence x=4.

practice.question: What step is supplied by Frobenius’s theorem rather than counting?
practice.hint: Identify the objects and the hypothesis needed before calculating.
practice.answer: A cardinality calculation alone cannot establish subgroup multiplication.

title: Fibers of a linear map become a vector space

source.title: MH3220 Algebra II — Kay Jin Lim, 25 July 2026

subject: Maps & quotients
intuition: Every fiber is a translated copy of the kernel. Replace that entire copy by one point and the map becomes a bijection onto its image.
explanation: Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map over a field. The quotient has vector addition and scalar multiplication inherited from $V$. If two representatives differ by a kernel vector, their images agree, so the displayed map is well-defined. Every image vector has a representative, and only the zero coset maps to zero.
proof: Prove well-definedness using $T(v-u)=0$. Linearity is inherited directly from $T$. Surjectivity follows from the definition of the image, and injectivity from equality of fibers. In finite dimensions, extend a basis of the kernel to a basis of $V$; the images of the new basis vectors form a basis of the image.
pitfall: The image can be a proper subspace of the stated codomain. Quotienting by the kernel gives the image, not automatically the whole codomain.
prompt: Predict how fiber size changes from rank zero to rank one to rank two over the displayed finite field.

worked.title: A projection over the field with three elements
steps: Let $T(x,y)=(x,0)$ over $\mathbb F_3$. The kernel contains $(0,0),(0,1),(0,2)$.
There are three fibers, indexed by $x$, each containing three vectors.
Thus the nine-element domain becomes a three-element quotient, isomorphic to the image line.

labScope: Change the controls to test this finite example. The calculation illustrates the stated result; the proof establishes its general scope. This experiment tests the displayed example; the lesson supplies the general argument.
objective: Build a basis of V/ker T and identify its image under the induced isomorphism.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

practice.question: For the worked projection over $\mathbb F_3$, what is the fiber over $(2,0)$?
practice.hint: Set the first coordinate to 2; the second coordinate is arbitrary in the field.
practice.answer: It is $(2,0)+\ker T=\{(2,t):t\in\mathbb F_3\}=\{(2,0),(2,1),(2,2)\}$. It is an affine coset, not a subspace because it does not contain zero.

title: One relation changes the arithmetic

source.title: MH3220 Algebra II — Kay Jin Lim, 25 July 2026

subject: Fields & polynomials
intuition: Adjoining a symbol becomes concrete when one polynomial relation tells you how to reduce every higher power.
explanation: Every residue class has a unique representative $u+v\alpha$, because the modulus is monic of degree two. The quotient therefore has $p^2$ elements. Addition works coefficient by coefficient. Multiplication expands first, then uses the defining relation. The same construction gives fields, products of fields, or rings with nilpotents depending on factorisation.
theorem: A\text{ a field}\iff X^2+bX+c\text{ irreducible over }\mathbb F_p.
proof: Polynomial division gives unique representatives. If the modulus is irreducible, every nonzero lower-degree polynomial is coprime to it; Bézout gives a multiplicative inverse in the quotient. If the modulus factors, its proper factors give nonzero classes whose product is zero. Repeated roots yield nilpotents; distinct roots yield a product by the Chinese remainder theorem.
pitfall: No roots implies irreducibility for degrees two and three. The same root test is insufficient in degree four or higher.
prompt: Over the field with three elements, compare a repeated-root modulus, a split modulus, and an irreducible quadratic.

worked.title: Three different rings of size nine
steps: $\mathbb F_3[X]/(X^2)$ has a nonzero nilpotent $\alpha$ with $\alpha^2=0$.
$X^2-1=(X-1)(X+1)$ gives $\mathbb F_3[X]/(X^2-1)\cong\mathbb F_3\times\mathbb F_3$.
$X^2+1$ has no root in $\mathbb F_3$, so its quotient is the field with nine elements.

labScope: Change the controls to test this finite example. The calculation illustrates the stated result; the proof establishes its general scope.
objective: Diagnose all three ring types from factorization of the modulus and verify the diagnosis arithmetically.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on column vectors; AB applies B first. Dₙ has 2n elements. Field and finiteness hypotheses belong to each statement.

practice.question: Which of the three rings contains a nonzero nilpotent?
practice.hint: A field or product of fields has no nonzero nilpotents.
practice.answer: The quotient by $X^2$ does. Its class of X is nonzero with square zero. Neither the field nor the split product has such an element.

subject: Modules & representations
objective: Carry the scalar-equality distinction into the external tensor product: reciprocal nonidentity scalars can cancel.
labScope: The eigenvalue argument above proves the general bound. A plotted or tabulated equality alone illustrates it; only equality of the actual trace with degree proves kernel membership.
conventions: Finite groups; nonzero finite-dimensional complex representations; left actions on column vectors. Products AB apply B first. D₈ has eight elements, with r⁴=s²=1 and srs=r⁻¹. intuition: Can a character have maximum absolute value away from the kernel?
explanation: For a finite group representation over C, π(g) has finite order and is diagonalizable. Its d eigenvalues lie on the unit circle. The triangle inequality gives the bound. The ordinary equality and absolute equality have different conclusions.
proof: If g has order m, π(g)^m=I. Over C, x^m−1 has distinct roots, so π(g) diagonalizes with mth-root eigenvalues ζ₁,…,ζ_d. Each |ζ_j|=1. The triangle inequality yields |Σζ_j|≤Σ|ζ_j|=d. If Σζ_j=d, all real parts must equal one, hence every ζ_j=1 and π(g)=I. If |Σζ_j|=d, equality in the triangle inequality makes all ζ_j share one phase λ, so π(g)=λI. The converse in each case is immediate.
pitfall: Never replace χ(g)=d by |χ(g)|=d in the kernel test: −I is scalar but not identity.
prompt: For the D₈ half-turn r², predict χ(r²), |χ(r²)| and whether r² is in the kernel.

worked.title: The central half-turn in the faithful D₈ plane action
steps: The square representation sends r² to −I₂.
Thus χ(r²)=−2 and |χ(r²)|=2=χ(1).
Yet r² is nonidentity and π(r²)≠I₂; it is not in the kernel.

practice.question: A degree-three finite-group representation has π(g)=ωI₃ with ω³=1 and ω≠1. What follows?
practice.hint: Check the exact field, factor action and theorem hypotheses before concluding.
practice.answer: χ(g)=3ω has absolute value 3, but 3ω≠3. This is a scalar preimage, not a kernel element.

title: External tensor products

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory
source.section: §15 The Character Table: row orthogonality; S₃ example

subject: Modules & representations
objective: Next factor inner products of these product characters to prove which external products are irreducible.
labScope: Kronecker trace multiplication and the group action law are proved in the lesson. The grid reports the selected finite examples and distinguishes the external group action from tensor balancing.
conventions: Finite groups; nonzero finite-dimensional complex representations; left actions on column vectors. Products AB apply B first. D₈ has eight elements, with r⁴=s²=1 and srs=r⁻¹. intuition: How can two different groups act on one tensor space?
explanation: For representations π of G on V and ρ of H on W, the product group acts on V⊗_C W. This is external because the two factors belong to different groups; the vector-space tensor is over C. It differs from balancing a right R-module with a left R-module over a ring.
proof: Define (g,h)·(v⊗w)=π(g)v⊗ρ(h)w and extend linearly; the tensor universal property makes this well-defined over C. For (g₁,h₁)(g₂,h₂)=(g₁g₂,h₁h₂), composing operators gives π(g₁)π(g₂)⊗ρ(h₁)ρ(h₂), so the action law holds. Inverse pairs act invertibly, and bases {v_i⊗w_j} show degree (dim V)(dim W). The diagonal entries of A⊗B are A_ii B_jj. Summing i,j gives tr(A⊗B)=tr(A)tr(B).
pitfall: Do not infer that faithful factors always give a faithful external tensor product; reciprocal scalars may cancel.
prompt: For π(a)=ω on C and ρ(r²)=−I₂, predict the product degree and trace at (a,r²).

worked.title: A C₃ character tensored with the D₈ plane
steps: Let a generate C₃ with π(a)=ω, and let ρ be the faithful two-dimensional D₈ square representation.
The product has degree 1·2=2; (a,r) acts by ωρ(r).
Since tr ρ(r)=0, the product character at (a,r) is ω·0=0.

practice.question: What happens to the pair (t,r²) in sign(C₂)⊠square(D₈)?
practice.hint: Check the exact field, factor action and theorem hypotheses before concluding.
practice.answer: The two negative scalar factors multiply to +1, so the pair is in the product kernel.

title: Irreducibles of direct products

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory
source.section: §15 The Character Table: row orthogonality; S₃ example
source.role: Background for character inner products; meeting reconstruction status in audit provenance

subject: Modules & representations
objective: Now one can test faithfulness of each irreducible product using the actual scalar-preimage kernel rather than factor kernels alone.
labScope: The lesson proves factorisation and completeness. The dashboard gives an exact count for the selected small groups; no picture substitutes for the character-inner-product proof.
conventions: Finite groups; nonzero finite-dimensional complex representations; left actions on column vectors. Products AB apply B first. D₈ has eight elements, with r⁴=s²=1 and srs=r⁻¹. This lesson reconstructs omitted proof steps from the supplied meeting notes; it is not a verbatim meeting transcript.
intuition: Could a direct product have an irreducible representation that is missing from the tensor list?
explanation: For finite groups over C, irreducible characters of G and H form orthonormal lists. External products give candidates for G×H. Factoring the product-group inner product proves each candidate irreducible. A sum of squared degrees equal to |G×H| leaves no missing irreducibles.
theorem: G,H\text{ finite; complex finite-dimensional representations}:\quad \langle\chi_i\psi_j,\chi_k\psi_\ell\rangle_{G\times H}=\delta_{ik}\delta_{j\ell},\quad \sum_{i,j}(d_i e_j)^2=|G||H|.
proof: Write χ_{i,j}(g,h)=χ_i(g)ψ_j(h). The inner-product sum over G×H separates into one sum over G and one over H. Each factor inner product is Kronecker delta, so the product is δ_{ik}δ_{jℓ}. This proves the candidates are irreducible and pairwise inequivalent. Compute Σ_{i,j}(d_i e_j)²=(Σ_i d_i²)(Σ_j e_j²)=|G||H|. For finite groups over C, all irreducible squared degrees sum to the group order. The candidates use the whole total, so no further irreducible can occur.
pitfall: The product character formula alone is not a completeness proof; the degree-squared sum is essential.
prompt: Predict the number and degree-squared total for C₃×D₈ before viewing the accounting table.

worked.title: All characters of C₂×C₃
steps: Each cyclic group has only degree-one complex irreducibles: two for C₂ and three for C₃.
Their six external products are pairwise distinct by factored orthogonality.
Six squared degrees sum to 6=|C₂×C₃|, so the six exhaust the irreducibles.

practice.question: If G has irreducible degrees 1,1,2 and H has degrees 1,1,1, how many product irreducibles and what total squared degree?
practice.hint: Check the exact field, factor action and theorem hypotheses before concluding.
practice.answer: There are 3·3=9 pairs; squared-degree sum is (1+1+4)(1+1+1)=18.

title: Scalar matching in product kernels

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory
source.section: §15 The Character Table: row orthogonality; S₃ example

subject: Modules & representations
objective: Schur turns these scalar preimages into central characters; compare their root-of-unity images to decide whether a product is faithful.
labScope: The pure-tensor argument in the lesson proves the exact formula. The table classifies every pair in the displayed finite example and marks scalar preimages separately from kernels.
conventions: Finite groups; nonzero finite-dimensional complex representations; left actions on column vectors. Products AB apply B first. D₈ has eight elements, with r⁴=s²=1 and srs=r⁻¹. This lesson reconstructs omitted proof steps from the supplied meeting notes; it is not a verbatim meeting transcript.
intuition: How can two nonidentity operators multiply to the identity on a tensor product?
explanation: The kernel of an external product includes factor-kernel pairs but can include more. For invertible matrices A,B on nonzero finite-dimensional spaces, A⊗B=I implies A and B are reciprocal scalars. For faithful irreducibles, those scalar preimages lie in the centers by faithfulness and Schur.
proof: Let A⊗B=I and choose nonzero w. For every v, Av⊗Bw=v⊗w; uniqueness of pure-tensor factors forces Av=λ_v v and Bw=λ_v⁻¹w. Since B and w are fixed, λ_v is constant for every nonzero v; linearity then gives A=λI and B=λ⁻¹I. Conversely reciprocal scalars tensor to I. Apply this operator statement to A=π(g), B=ρ(h) to obtain the exact kernel set. If π is faithful and π(g) is scalar, it commutes with every π(x); faithfulness forces g to commute with every x, so g∈Z(G). Repeat for H. This center conclusion needs faithfulness.
pitfall: Never compute the product kernel as kerπ×kerρ without checking nontrivial scalar preimages.
prompt: Choose C₂ or C₃ with the D₈ square representation. Predict whether a nonidentity product pair acts as identity.

worked.title: Cancellation in C₂×D₈
steps: The faithful C₂ sign has π(t)=−1 and the faithful D₈ plane has ρ(r²)=−I₂.
The scalar pair is (−1,−1), whose product is +1.
Thus (t,r²) is a nonidentity product-kernel element although both individual kernels are trivial.

practice.question: Why is faithful(C₃)⊠faithful(D₈ square) faithful?
practice.hint: Check the exact field, factor action and theorem hypotheses before concluding.
practice.answer: The reciprocal scalar sets intersect only at 1. Faithful factors alone do not suffice, as C₂×D₈ shows.

title: When is a product irreducible faithful?

source.title: Jerome Queck · From Group Theory to Representation Theory
source.section: §15 The Character Table: row orthogonality; S₃ example

subject: Modules & representations
objective: The representation route now joins Maschke, Schur, character inner products, tables, external products and the scalar-compatibility capstone.
labScope: The centre-character argument proves the finite complex criterion. The compatibility table checks these examples and cannot replace the proof that all product irreducibles have this form.
conventions: Finite groups; nonzero finite-dimensional complex representations; left actions on column vectors. Products AB apply B first. D₈ has eight elements, with r⁴=s²=1 and srs=r⁻¹. This lesson reconstructs omitted proof steps from the supplied meeting notes; it is not a verbatim meeting transcript.
intuition: Exactly when can faithful irreducibles of two groups combine faithfully?
definition: G\times H\text{ has a faithful irreducible over }\mathbb C\iff G,H\text{ each do and }\gcd(|Z(G)|,|Z(H)|)=1
explanation: For finite groups over C, every irreducible of G×H is an external tensor of irreducibles. If the factors are faithful, Schur sends each center injectively to roots of unity. Their common scalar subgroup has size gcd of center orders and indexes the product kernel. Necessity follows because a faithful product restricts faithfully to each factor.
proof: For faithful irreducible π, Schur gives π(z)=α(z)I for z∈Z(G). Faithfulness makes α injective; similarly β for H. Finite subgroups of C× are cyclic. The images are μ_a and μ_b, where a=|Z(G)| and b=|Z(H)|. Their intersection has gcd(a,b) elements. Each common scalar gives exactly one central pair with α(z)β(w)=1, so |ker(π⊠ρ)|=gcd(a,b). Thus coprime centers and faithful factors suffice. Conversely, a faithful irreducible of G×H is π⊠ρ by the previous lesson. If either factor had a kernel, its product with identity would lie in the product kernel. Both factors are faithful, and the same gcd formula forces coprime center orders.
pitfall: Coprime center orders are sufficient only with faithful irreducible factors; a cyclic center alone does not assert that a factor has one.
prompt: Predict the difference between C₂×D₈ and C₃×D₈ before checking center orders and kernel pairs.

worked.title: C₂×D₈ fails
steps: The sign of C₂ is faithful and the geometric D₈ plane is faithful irreducible.
Their center orders are 2 and 2; the common scalar −1 gives (t,r²) in the tensor kernel.
Every irreducible of C₂×D₈ is a product, so no alternative faithful irreducible escapes this obstruction.

practice.question: Which product admits a faithful irreducible with D₈: C₂×D₈ or C₃×D₈?
practice.hint: Check the exact field, factor action and theorem hypotheses before concluding.
practice.answer: D₈ has a faithful irreducible with center order 2. The C₃ center order is coprime to 2; the C₂ order is not.

title: Coset coordinates and Mackey orbit pieces
navTitle: Coset coordinates and Mackey orbit pieces
section: Section 16, Mackey restriction and irreducibility, Theorem 16.2 and Corollary 16.7

source.title: CT, Representation Theory, Lent 2005
source.section: Section 16, Mackey restriction and irreducibility, Theorem 16.2 and Corollary 16.7
source.role: Independent primary mathematical reference. Original tensor-coordinate proof here.

subject: Representations & symmetry

worked.title: Two orbit pieces in S3
steps: Take $G=S_3$, $H=K=\langle(12)\rangle$, and choose $g=(13)$. The three left $K$-cosets form one fixed $H$-orbit $K$ and one orbit of size two containing $gK$. Thus $D=\{1,g\}$.

For $g=1$, $L_1=H$. For $g=(13)$, $gKg^{-1}=\langle(23)\rangle$, so $L_g=1$. The induced module has one coordinate in the first piece and two in the second. For a one-dimensional $V$, these pieces have dimensions one and two.

objective: Construct unique induced-module coordinates and identify the subgroup controlling each restricted orbit.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the named objects and maps. It does not compute tensors or prove the general theorem.
conventions: All group actions are left actions. Matrices act on columns and the rightmost map acts first. Each statement declares its coefficient ring or field.
intuition: A restricted induced module separates according to the orbits of H on its coset coordinates. The stabilizer of a coordinate determines the action within that coordinate.
definition: U=RG\otimes_{RK}V,\qquad L_g=H\cap gKg^{-1},\qquad W_g=\bigoplus_{tK\subset HgK}t\otimes V
explanation: Let $G$ be finite, $H,K\le G$, $R$ a unital ring and $V$ a unital left $RK$-module with action $\sigma$. Group symbols commute with coefficients in the ordinary group ring. The tensor module $U=RG\otimes_{RK}V$ is a left $RH$-module by restriction. A representative $t\in G$, a coset $tK\subset G$, and a coordinate copy $t\otimes V\subset U$ have different types. Choose a left-coset transversal $T$ for $G/K$. The expression $\sum_{t\in T}t\otimes v_t$ is a unique coordinate expansion. For $h\in H$, write $ht=t^{\prime}k$ with $k\in K$. Then $h(t\otimes v)=t^{\prime}\otimes\sigma(k)v$. Thus the orbit of $gK$ indexes an invariant summand $W_g$. No semisimplicity or basis of $V$ is needed.
proof: Every group element has a unique expression $tk$ with $t\in T$, $k\in K$. Consequently every $b\in RG$ has a unique finite expansion $b=\sum_t t q_t(b)$ with $q_t(b)\in RK$. The coefficient maps are additive and satisfy $q_t(ba)=q_t(b)a$ for $a\in RK$. This follows first on group symbols and then on sums, preserving coefficient order. Define $\Theta:\bigoplus_T V\to U$ by $\Theta((v_t))=\sum_t t\otimes v_t$. Define $P(b\otimes v)=(q_t(b)v)_t$. To descend $P$ to the tensor quotient, check $q_t(ba)v=q_t(b)(av)$. Additivity in each variable is immediate. Thus $P$ is well-defined, and $P\Theta((v_t))=(v_t)$ while $\Theta P(b\otimes v)=\sum_t t\otimes q_t(b)v=b\otimes v$. These identities prove unique coordinates without assuming tensor products preserve arbitrary injections. For $h\in H$ and $t\in T$, the unique factorization $ht=t^{\prime}k$ gives $h(t\otimes v)=t^{\prime}\otimes\sigma(k)v$. This moves a coordinate only within its $H$-orbit on $G/K$. The orbits are indexed by double cosets $H\backslash G/K$, because $aK$ and $bK$ lie in the same orbit exactly when $b=hak$ for some $h\in H,k\in K$. Choose a representative set $D$ for those double cosets. Partition the transversal $T$ by these orbits. Grouping the unique coordinates gives $U=\bigoplus_{g\in D}W_g$. Every $W_g$ is $RH$-invariant by the action formula. The sum is onto because every coordinate occurs, and direct because the coordinate subsets are disjoint and $P$ detects every coordinate. The stabilizer in $H$ of $gK$ consists of $x$ with $xgK=gK$. This is equivalent to $g^{-1}xg\in K$, so it is exactly $L_g=H\cap gKg^{-1}$. The map $H/L_g\to H\cdot(gK)$ is well-defined. Equality $agK=bgK$ is equivalent to $b^{-1}a\in L_g$, which proves injectivity, and every orbit point has form $agK$, which proves surjectivity. Conjugation $x\mapsto g^{-1}xg$ identifies $L_g$ with $K\cap g^{-1}Hg$. Hence the correct left $RL_g$-action on the vector or module underlying $V$ is $x\cdot_g v=\sigma(g^{-1}xg)v$, extended additively with the original $R$-action. Since conjugation preserves multiplication, this is a module action. The next lesson reconstructs the whole $W_g$ by inducing this action to $H$.
pitfall: Cosets are not group elements. The set $HgK$ need not be a subgroup. Disjoint group subsets alone do not prove a tensor sum direct; unique tensor coordinates do.
prompt: Follow the coordinate to its H-orbit, then identify the stabilizer action inside that coordinate.

practice.question: Which assumption is needed for the orbit decomposition over an ordinary group ring?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: A unital $RK$-module and the declared subgroup actions. Unique coset coordinates and their $H$-orbits construct the decomposition. Averaging and Schur are not used.

practice.question: For $H=K=\langle(12)\rangle\le S_3$ and $g=(13)$, what is $L_g$?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: The trivial subgroup. The conjugate subgroup is generated by $(23)$, whose intersection with $\langle(12)\rangle$ is trivial.

practice.question: What proves that the sum over double-coset pieces is direct?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: The inverse coordinate map $P$ detects each coordinate independently. The explicit isomorphism with $\bigoplus_T V$ gives unique coordinates. Double cosets need not be subgroups.
