worked.title: Restrict an induced sign module in S3
steps: Let $H=K=\langle s\rangle$ with $s=(12)$ and let $V=\mathbb C$ carry $s\mapsto-1$. The two Mackey representatives are $1$ and $(13)$, with intersections $H$ and $1$.

The first summand is $V$. The second is $\mathbb CH\otimes_{\mathbb C}V$, a regular $H$-module of dimension two. Hence the restriction is $\operatorname{sgn}_H\oplus\mathbb CH$. At $1$ its trace is three and at $s$ its trace is $-1+0=-1$.
Choose $A_{(13)}=\{1,s\}$. The inverse sends $(13)\otimes z+s(13)\otimes w$ to $1\otimes z+s\otimes w$. This identifies the two moving coordinates explicitly.

objective: Prove Mackey restriction of induction with balancing, inverse coordinates, naturality and representative changes.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the named objects and maps. It does not compute tensors or prove the general theorem.
conventions: All group actions are left actions. Matrices act on columns and the rightmost map acts first. Each statement declares its coefficient ring or field.
intuition: The map carries a stabilizer coordinate at a to the original induced coordinate at ag. The twist is exactly what makes this map balanced.
explanation: Keep $G,H,K,R,V,D$ as in the preceding lesson. For $g\in D$, let $L_g=H\cap gKg^{-1}$ and let ${}^gV$ denote $V$ with the left $L_g$-action $xv=\sigma(g^{-1}xg)v$. The proposed map is $\Phi_g:RH\otimes_{RL_g}{}^gV\to W_g\subset RG\otimes_{RK}V$. For each $g$, select a transversal $A_g$ of $H/L_g$. The elements $ag$ with $a\in A_g$ represent precisely the $K$-cosets inside $HgK$. Together over $D$, these elements form a transversal for $G/K$. They supply inverse coordinates and prove the full map bijective.
proof: For a group element $x\in L_g$, $xg=g(g^{-1}xg)$. Thus $axg\otimes v=ag\otimes\sigma(g^{-1}xg)v$. For $q=\sum_x r_xx\in RL_g$, expand the sum to obtain $aqg\otimes v=ag\otimes\sum_x r_x\sigma(g^{-1}xg)v=ag\otimes(q\cdot_gv)$. Group symbols commute with coefficients, but coefficients have not been commuted with one another. This proves balancing for every subgroup-ring element. Additivity supplies a well-defined map $\Phi_g$. Left $RH$-linearity follows on pure tensors from $\Phi_g(ca\otimes v)=cag\otimes v=c\Phi_g(a\otimes v)$ and extends to sums. Its image lies in $W_g$ because $ag\in HgK$. The images of the $A_g$-coordinates cover all coordinates in $W_g$ by the coset bijection proved earlier. Use the adapted transversal $T=\coprod_{g\in D}A_gg$. Every element of $W_g$ has a unique expression $\sum_{a\in A_g}ag\otimes v_a$. Define $\Psi_g$ on this expression by $\Psi_g(\sum_a ag\otimes v_a)=\sum_a a\otimes v_a$. The same unique-coordinate theorem applies to $RH\otimes_{RL_g}{}^gV$, so this is a well-defined additive map and $\Psi_g\Phi_g$ and $\Phi_g\Psi_g$ fix every coordinate. Hence $\Phi_g$ is bijective. Its inverse is $RH$-linear because the inverse of a bijective $RH$-linear map is $RH$-linear. One can evaluate the inverse on a nonadapted group tensor directly. If $b=h g k$ with $h\in H,k\in K$, then $b\otimes v=hg\otimes\sigma(k)v$, so $\Psi_g(b\otimes v)=h\otimes\sigma(k)v$. If also $b=h^{\prime}gk^{\prime}$, then $x=h^{-1}h^{\prime}=gkk^{\prime-1}g^{-1}\in L_g$. Balancing gives $h^{\prime}\otimes\sigma(k^{\prime})v=hx\otimes\sigma(k^{\prime})v=h\otimes\sigma(g^{-1}xg)\sigma(k^{\prime})v=h\otimes\sigma(k)v$. Thus the formula agrees for every factorization. The direct sum $\Phi=\bigoplus_g\Phi_g$ is an $RH$-module isomorphism onto $\bigoplus_gW_g=\operatorname{Res}_H^G U$. For an $RK$-map $f:V\to V^{\prime}$, the two routes send $a\otimes v$ to $ag\otimes f(v)$. Because $f$ also intertwines the twisted $L_g$-actions, all maps are typed. This proves naturality in $V$. For another representative $g^{\prime}=h_0gk_0$, the stabilizer is $L_{g^{\prime}}=h_0L_gh_0^{-1}$. Define $J:RH\otimes_{RL_g}{}^gV\to RH\otimes_{RL_{g^{\prime}}}{}^{g^{\prime}}V$ by $J(a\otimes v)=ah_0^{-1}\otimes\sigma(k_0^{-1})v$. For $x\in L_g$, put $x^{\prime}=h_0xh_0^{-1}$. The equality ${}^{g^{\prime}}\sigma(x^{\prime})=\sigma(k_0^{-1}){}^g\sigma(x)\sigma(k_0)$ proves balancing of $J$, first on $x$ and then on sums. Its inverse is $J^{-1}(a^{\prime}\otimes w)=a^{\prime}h_0\otimes\sigma(k_0)w$. Applying the two formulas successively cancels $h_0$ and $k_0$, so both composites are the identity. Finally $\Phi_{g^{\prime}}J(a\otimes v)=agk_0\otimes\sigma(k_0^{-1})v=ag\otimes v$. The internal piece is independent of the chosen representative.
pitfall: The notation ${}^gV$ requires its acting subgroup. There is generally no action of all $H$ on this copy of $V$. The theorem is a module isomorphism, not merely an equality of character values.
prompt: Check the balancing relation at an arbitrary element of the subgroup ring, then follow one unique coordinate through both maps.

practice.question: Does the proof require a semisimple coefficient field?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: No. It uses coset coordinates over the declared unital ring. The explicit maps and coordinate inverses work before any decomposition into irreducibles.

practice.question: In the S3 sign example, what is the restricted module?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $\operatorname{sgn}_H\oplus\mathbb CH$. The intersection terms have dimensions one and two. The second intersection is trivial, so its induction is regular.

practice.question: If $g^{\prime}=h_0gk_0$, which comparison is compatible with the maps into $U$?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $a\otimes v\mapsto ah_0^{-1}\otimes\sigma(k_0^{-1})v$. The inverse factors cancel in $ah_0^{-1}g^{\prime}\otimes\sigma(k_0^{-1})v=ag\otimes v$.

worked.title: Two copies create four endomorphism parameters
steps: Let $S$ be an irreducible complex $G$-module and $U=S\oplus S$. Every equivariant endomorphism is a block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}aI&bI\\cI&dI\end{pmatrix}$ by Schur.

The four scalar parameters give $\dim\operatorname{End}_G(U)=4$. Projection onto the first copy is a nonscalar idempotent. Its presence detects reducibility even when both summands have the same character.

objective: Prove the complex semisimple endomorphism criterion and locate its field and characteristic boundaries.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the named objects and maps. It does not compute tensors or prove the general theorem.
conventions: All group actions are left actions. Matrices act on columns and the rightmost map acts first. Each statement declares its coefficient ring or field.
intuition: Irreducibility makes every equivariant endomorphism scalar. Complete reducibility makes every proper submodule visible through a nonscalar equivariant projection.
explanation: Let $G$ be finite and $U\ne0$ a finite-dimensional complex left $G$-module. Its commutant is the complex vector space $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb CG}(U)$ of linear maps $T$ with $T\rho(g)=\rho(g)T$ for every $g$. A projection onto an invariant subspace is an endomorphism only if its complement is also invariant. Over $\mathbb C$, every linear endomorphism has an eigenvalue. Schur uses that eigenvalue to prove scalarity. Conversely, averaging a projection onto a nonzero proper submodule produces a nontrivial equivariant idempotent. That averaging requires $|G|$ to be invertible.
proof: Suppose $U$ is irreducible and $T\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb CG}(U)$. Since $U$ is nonzero and finite-dimensional over $\mathbb C$, $T$ has an eigenvalue $\lambda$. The kernel of $T-\lambda I$ is a nonzero $G$-submodule. Irreducibility makes it all of $U$, so $T=\lambda I$. Scalar maps are equivariant, and $I\ne0$, so the endomorphism space has dimension exactly one. Conversely, suppose $W$ is a nonzero proper submodule. Choose an ordinary vector-space projection $p:U\to W$ with $p|_W=I_W$. Define $P=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}\rho(g)p\rho(g)^{-1}$. Every term has image in $W$ and restricts to the identity on $W$, so the same is true of $P$. Reindexing the sum proves $\rho(h)P\rho(h)^{-1}=P$ for every $h$. Thus $P$ is equivariant and $P^2=P$. The projection $P$ is neither zero nor the identity. A scalar idempotent over a field is zero or the identity, so $P$ is nonscalar. Therefore $I$ and $P$ are linearly independent equivariant endomorphisms. This contradicts dimension one. The contradiction proves the converse. The more general complex semisimple calculation is $U\cong\bigoplus_i S_i^{\oplus m_i}$ with pairwise nonisomorphic irreducibles. A map between distinct $S_i$ vanishes by Schur, while maps among $m_i$ equivalent copies form $M_{m_i}(\mathbb C)$. Hence $\operatorname{End}_G(U)\cong\bigoplus_iM_{m_i}(\mathbb C)$ as algebras and its dimension is $\sum_i m_i^2$. Here the block algebra statement is valid because the decomposition is an isotypic decomposition. This is different from a later adjunction isomorphism that merely identifies vector spaces. Over $\mathbb R$, let $C_4$ act on $\mathbb R^2$ by $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. There is no real invariant line because $J$ has no real eigenvalue. Solving $TJ=JT$ gives $T=aI+bJ$, so the irreducible module has a two-dimensional real commutant. Algebraic closure was essential to the scalar conclusion. In characteristic three, let $S_3$ act on $\mathbb F_3^2$ by $r=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $s=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. The relations $r^3=s^2=I$ and $srs=r^{-1}$ hold. The first coordinate line is invariant, so the module is reducible. A matrix commuting with $s$ is diagonal, and commuting also with $r$ makes its diagonal entries equal. Its commutant is one-dimensional. This disproves the converse without semisimplicity.
pitfall: A division endomorphism ring need not have dimension one over a nonclosed field. A scalar commutant need not force irreducibility in a nonsemisimple category.
prompt: Identify where the eigenvalue and the averaged projection enter the two implications.

edges: Schur and an eigenvalue over $\mathbb C$
a proper summand would give a nonscalar map

practice.question: Which step uses semisimplicity?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: Constructing an equivariant projection onto a proper submodule. The averaged projection requires division by $|G|$. It supplies the invariant complement used by the converse.

practice.question: For $U=S^{\oplus2}\oplus T$ with $S,T$ distinct complex irreducibles, what is $\dim\operatorname{End}_G(U)$?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: 5. The isotypic blocks are $M_2(\mathbb C)$ and $\mathbb C$, so the dimension is $2^2+1^2=5$.

practice.question: What does the characteristic-three S3 example show?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: A scalar commutant alone can coexist with reducibility without semisimplicity. The invariant line and scalar commutant refute precisely the unrestricted converse. They do not establish a claim about every induction criterion.

worked.title: The two-dimensional irreducible of S3 from A3
steps: Let $H=A_3=\langle r=(123)\rangle$, $G=S_3$ and $V=\mathbb C_\zeta$ with $r\mapsto\zeta$, where $\zeta$ is a nontrivial cube root. The two cosets have representatives $1,s=(12)$.
Conjugation by $s$ inverts $r$, so ${}^sV$ has character $\zeta^{-1}\ne\zeta$. The criterion proves $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G V$ irreducible of dimension two.

In the basis $1\otimes1,s\otimes1$, $r$ acts by $\operatorname{diag}(\zeta,\zeta^{-1})$ and $s$ swaps the two coordinates. The two distinct $r$-eigenlines are exchanged by $s$, which also gives a direct irreducibility check.

objective: Prove both directions of the normal-subgroup irreducibility criterion and compare representatives correctly.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the named objects and maps. It does not compute tensors or prove the general theorem.
conventions: All group actions are left actions. Matrices act on columns and the rightmost map acts first. Each statement declares its coefficient ring or field.
intuition: Only intertwiners from V to its conjugates contribute to the induced commutant. One identity contribution and no others give an irreducible complex module.
explanation: Let $G$ be finite, $H\trianglelefteq G$, and $0<\dim_{\mathbb C}V<\infty$ with $H$-action $\sigma$. Put $U=\mathbb CG\otimes_{\mathbb CH}V$. Choose $T$ for $G/H$ with $1\in T$. Write ${}^tV$ for $V$ with $h\mapsto\sigma(t^{-1}ht)$. Normality makes this action defined on every $h\in H$. The displayed isomorphism comes from induction-restriction adjunction followed by the restricted coset decomposition. It is not an algebra isomorphism with componentwise multiplication. The identity-coset contribution is $\operatorname{End}_H(V)$ and has dimension at least one.
theorem: \operatorname{Ind}_H^G V\text{ irreducible}\iff V\text{ irreducible and }{}^gV\not\cong V\text{ for all }g\in G\setminus H
proof:
For $h\in H$, normality gives $ht=t(t^{-1}ht)$ with $t^{-1}ht\in H$. Hence $h(t\otimes v)=t\otimes\sigma(t^{-1}ht)v$. Unique coordinates therefore identify $\operatorname{Res}_H^G U\cong igoplus_{t\in T}{}^tV$ as $H$-modules. Induction-restriction adjunction sends $F\in\operatorname{End}_G(U)$ to $v\mapsto F(1\otimes v)$ in $\operatorname{Hom}_H(V,\operatorname{Res}U)$. Its inverse sends an $H$-map $f$ to $b\otimes v\mapsto bf(v)$. The inverse is balanced because $bhf(v)=bf(hv)$. Both composites fix pure tensors or their evaluations. Composing with the finite-sum coordinate projections gives the displayed vector-space isomorphism and its dimension formula. Assume first that $U$ is irreducible. The complex endomorphism criterion makes the total dimension one. The $t=1$ term is $\operatorname{End}_H(V)$, which contains the nonzero identity. Thus it has dimension one and every other Hom term vanishes. The same endomorphism criterion for the finite group $H$ now proves $V$ irreducible. Conjugation is an automorphism of $H$, so every ${}^tV$ is irreducible. Schur says a nonzero Hom between these irreducibles would be an isomorphism. Therefore ${}^tV
ot\cong V$ for each $t
e1$. Conversely, suppose $V$ is irreducible and every nonidentity representative gives a nonisomorphic conjugate. All ${}^tV$ are irreducible, so Schur gives $\dim\operatorname{End}_H(V)=1$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_H(V,{}^tV)=0$ for $t
e1$. The total endomorphism dimension of $U$ is one. Since $U$ is a nonzero finite-dimensional complex finite-group module, the semisimple converse proves $U$ irreducible. To replace representatives by all elements outside $H$, let $g^{\prime}=gh_0$ with $h_0\in H$. The invertible map $A=\sigma(h_0^{-1})$ satisfies $A\sigma(g^{-1}hg)=\sigma(g^{\prime-1}hg^{\prime})A$ for every $h\in H$. Hence ${}^gV\cong{}^{g^{\prime}}V$. The nonisomorphism condition is constant on a coset. The identity coset gives conjugates isomorphic to $V$ by the same calculation. Normality and complex semisimplicity have distinct jobs. Without normality, conjugation need not preserve $H$ and Mackey intersections replace full conjugates. Over $\mathbb R$, an irreducible module can have a larger division commutant, so the one-dimensional criterion used here cannot prove the same equivalence.
pitfall: Nonisomorphic reducible modules may have nonzero Hom. Apply Schur only after proving $V$ and its conjugates irreducible. The theorem here is over $\mathbb C$, not a field-free assertion.
prompt: Separate the identity coset in the endomorphism sum before using Schur.

edges: dimension one means every other term vanishes

practice.question: Why can this proof conclude irreducibility from total endomorphism dimension one?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: The module is nonzero, finite-dimensional and complex, and the finite group gives semisimplicity. The preceding criterion applies under exactly these hypotheses. The adjunction decomposition is only a vector-space statement.

practice.question: For nontrivial $\mathbb C_\zeta$ of $A_3$, which conjugate is obtained from a transposition?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $\mathbb C_{\zeta^{-1}}$, so induction is irreducible. A transposition conjugates a 3-cycle to its inverse, and nontrivial cube roots are distinct from their inverses.

practice.question: If the induced module is irreducible, what must be shown before applying Schur to the conjugate terms?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: The identity term has dimension one, hence $V$ is irreducible by semisimplicity. Only after $V$ is known irreducible are its conjugates irreducible and Schur applicable.

worked.title: A3 and A4 separate a 3-cycle from its inverse
steps: In $S_3$, $x=(123)$ has centralizer $\langle x\rangle$ of order three, all even. Its $S_3$-class of size two splits into two singleton classes in the abelian group $A_3$.
In $S_4$, the centralizer remains $\langle(123)\rangle$, because the single fixed point must remain fixed. The $S_4$-class has size $24/3=8$ and splits into two $A_4$-classes of size four.
The inverse $(132)$ is obtained by the odd conjugator $(23)$. Every other conjugator differs from it by an even centralizer element, so no even conjugator sends $(123)$ to $(132)$.

objective: Prove the index-two centralizer test, equal class sizes and the odd-conjugator repair.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the declared objects and relationships. It is not an algebraic solver or a general-proof animation.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on columns. Inner products are linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second.
intuition: The even and odd conjugators give at most two alternating-group classes. An odd centralizer element makes those two sets coincide.
explanation: Let $n\ge2$, $G=S_n$, $N=A_n$ and $x\in A_n$. The conjugacy class $x^G=\{gxg^{-1}:g\in G\}$ lies inside $A_n$, since sign is unchanged by conjugation. Its centralizer is $C_G(x)=\{c:cx=xc\}$. We compare the conjugation actions of $G$ and its index-two normal subgroup $N$. Conjugating by a fixed odd $\tau$ carries the $A_n$-class of $x$ bijectively to the other possible $A_n$-class. They coincide precisely when the centralizer contains an odd permutation. If they do not coincide, they are disjoint equal-sized orbits.
theorem: x^{S_n}\text{ splits into two }A_n\text{-classes}\iff C_{S_n}(x)\subseteq A_n
proof: Fix an odd $\tau\in S_n$. Every permutation lies in $A_n$ or $\tau A_n$. Therefore $x^{S_n}=x^{A_n}\cup\tau x^{A_n}\tau^{-1}$. Normality of $A_n$ shows that the second set is the $A_n$-conjugacy class of $\tau x\tau^{-1}$. Orbits under a group action are equal or disjoint, so there are at most two classes. If an odd $c$ centralizes $x$, every odd conjugator $g$ can be replaced by the even $gc^{-1}$. Indeed $(gc^{-1})x(gc^{-1})^{-1}=gxg^{-1}$. This repair proves that every $S_n$-conjugate is already an $A_n$-conjugate, so there is only one class. Conversely, if $\tau x\tau^{-1}=axa^{-1}$ for some even $a$, then $a^{-1}\tau$ centralizes $x$ and is odd. Hence equality of the two possible classes forces an odd centralizer element. If the centralizer has no odd element, the classes are disjoint. The map $y\mapsto\tau y\tau^{-1}$ is a bijection between the two classes, so their sizes are equal. The orbit-stabilizer calculation makes the size precise. If $C_{S_n}(x)\subset A_n$, then $C_{A_n}(x)=C_{S_n}(x)$ and $|x^{A_n}|=(n!/2)/|C_{S_n}(x)|=|x^{S_n}|/2$. If there is an odd centralizer element, sign restricts onto $\{1,-1\}$ on the centralizer, giving $|C_{S_n}(x)|=2|C_{A_n}(x)|$ and equal $S_n$ and $A_n$ class sizes. This argument works for any index-two normal subgroup $N\trianglelefteq G$ and $x\in N$. The test is $C_G(x)\subseteq N$. For alternating groups, the next lesson identifies this condition directly from all cycle lengths, including length-one cycles.
pitfall: The theorem applies to an even permutation and asks about conjugacy under A_n. It does not say that every S_n class splits, or that the two parts have different cycle types.
prompt: Try to repair an odd conjugator by multiplying it on the right by an odd element that centralizes x.

practice.question: What is the correct splitting test for $x\in A_n$?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: Every element of $C_{S_n}(x)$ is even. An odd centralizer repairs an odd conjugator. Its absence leaves exactly two disjoint classes.

practice.question: How large are the two A4 classes of 3-cycles?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: Four each. The S4 class has size $24/3=8$, and the splitting test halves it.

practice.question: Given an odd conjugator $g$ and an odd centralizer element $c$, which even conjugator gives the same image of $x$?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $gc^{-1}$. The product $gc^{-1}$ is even and its conjugation of $x$ equals that of $g$ because $c$ centralizes $x$.

worked.title: A5, A6 and A7 see different fixed-point counts
steps: The 5-cycle $(12345)$ has full types $(5)$ in $S_5$, $(5,1)$ in $S_6$ and $(5,1,1)$ in $S_7$. The first two have distinct odd parts, while the last repeats one.
In $A_5$, the 24 5-cycles split into classes of size 12. In $A_6$, the $720/5=144$ elements of type $(5,1)$ split into classes of size 72.
In $A_7$, $(67)$ is an odd centralizer for the same written 5-cycle. The type $(5,1,1)$ has centralizer order $5\cdot2=10$ in $S_7$, and its 504 elements form one $A_7$-class.

objective: Prove the full cycle-length splitting criterion and apply the repeated-fixed-point obstruction.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the declared objects and relationships. It is not an algebraic solver or a general-proof animation.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on columns. Inner products are linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second.
intuition: An even cycle or a swap of two equal odd cycles produces an odd centralizer. With distinct odd lengths, every centralizer is a product of even cycle powers.
definition: x=c_1\cdots c_r,\qquad \ell_i=|c_i|\quad\text{with every fixed point included as }\ell_i=1
explanation: Let $x\in A_n$ with $n\ge2$. Write its disjoint cycles on all $n$ letters, including every fixed point. A centralizing permutation sends an $\langle x\rangle$-orbit to another orbit of the same size and respects the cyclic order. The sign of an $\ell$-cycle is $(-1)^{\ell-1}$. A swap of two disjoint cycles of length $\ell$ has sign $(-1)^\ell$. Those facts detect every obstruction to the centralizer being contained in $A_n$.
theorem: x^{S_n}\text{ splits in }A_n\iff \ell_1,\ldots,\ell_r\text{ are distinct odd integers}
proof: If $x$ has a disjoint cycle $c$ of even length, $c$ commutes with every other disjoint cycle and hence with $x$. Since $\operatorname{sgn}(c)=(-1)^{|c|-1}=-1$, the centralizer contains an odd element. The class does not split. If two disjoint cycles of the same odd length are $c=(a_0\ldots a_{\ell-1})$ and $d=(b_0\ldots b_{\ell-1})$, define $s=\prod_{j=0}^{\ell-1}(a_jb_j)$. Conjugation by $s$ interchanges $c$ and $d$ and fixes the other cycles, so $sxs^{-1}=x$. There are $\ell$ disjoint transpositions in $s$, so it is odd. For $\ell=1$, this is exactly the transposition of two fixed points. Thus any repeated odd length also prevents splitting. Conversely, suppose the full cycle lengths are distinct and odd. A permutation $z$ commuting with $x$ satisfies $z(x^j a)=x^jz(a)$. Therefore it maps each $x$-orbit to an orbit of the same length. Distinct lengths force every orbit to map to itself. On a cycle $c$ of length $\ell$, the choice $z(a)=c^t(a)$ forces $z(c^ja)=c^{j+t}(a)$ at every point. Thus the restriction of $z$ to that support is $c^t$. Consequently the entire centralizer consists of products of powers of the disjoint cycles. Every odd-length cycle is even, as is each power and each product. Hence $C_{S_n}(x)\subseteq A_n$, and the class splits. This proof also computes $|C_{S_n}(x)|=\prod_i\ell_i$ in the distinct-length case. The split classes then have size $n!/(2\prod_i\ell_i)$. In a general type with $m_\ell$ cycles of length $\ell$, commuting permutations can rotate each cycle and permute the cycles of equal length, giving $|C_{S_n}(x)|=\prod_\ell\ell^{m_\ell}m_\ell!$. Each rotation and each cycle permutation is determined by the images of orbit representatives, which proves the count.
pitfall: The phrase "all cycles are odd" is insufficient. Repeated odd cycles, including two fixed points, prevent splitting. This theorem concerns all $n$ letters.
prompt: Write the full cycle type before checking parity or distinctness.

edges: even cycle or repeated odd length gives an obstruction

practice.question: Which full cycle type can split?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $(5,1)$. Only $(5,1)$ has all lengths odd and distinct. Repeated ones are repeated odd cycles.

practice.question: Does the type $(3,3)$ split in A6?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: No. Swapping its two cycles gives three transpositions and an odd centralizer. The explicit swap $(14)(25)(36)$ commutes with $(123)(456)$ and is odd.

practice.question: Under distinct odd cycle lengths, why is every centralizer element even?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: It preserves each cycle support and acts there by a power of that odd-length cycle. Distinct lengths fix the supports. Commutation determines a cycle rotation on each support, and those rotations are even.

worked.title: A rectangular complex adjoint
steps: On the standard Hermitian spaces, let $A:\mathbb C^2\to\mathbb C$ be $A(x_1,x_2)=2x_1+ix_2$. Its matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}2&i\end{pmatrix}$.
The adjoint has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-i\end{pmatrix}$, so $A^*y=(2y,-iy)$. Directly, $\langle x,A^*y\rangle=2x_1\overline y+ix_2\overline y=\langle Ax,y\rangle$.

objective: Construct a finite-dimensional adjoint, prove uniqueness and linearity, and extend basis-pair equations to all vectors.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the declared objects and relationships. It is not an algebraic solver or a general-proof animation.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on columns. Inner products are linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second.
intuition: For each target vector y, the expression paired with Ax is a linear functional in x. Nondegeneracy identifies the one vector A*y that represents that functional.
explanation: Let $X,Y$ be finite-dimensional inner-product spaces over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and $A:X\to Y$ linear. We use $\langle\alpha x,y\rangle=\alpha\langle x,y\rangle$ and $\langle x,\alpha y\rangle=\overline\alpha\langle x,y\rangle$. The adjoint has type $A^*:Y\to X$ and satisfies $\langle Ax,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_X$. Choose orthonormal bases $e_i$ of $X$ and $f_j$ of $Y$. The column matrix $M=[A]$ has entries $M_{ji}=\langle Ae_i,f_j\rangle$. The matrix of the adjoint in the reversed bases is $M^\dagger=\overline M^T$. The orthonormality assumption belongs to this matrix shortcut.
proof: For an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ of $X$, define $B(y)=\sum_i\langle y,Ae_i\rangle_Y e_i$. Each coefficient is linear in $y$, so $B:Y\to X$ is linear. If $X$ is zero, the empty sum gives its unique map and the same argument applies. Write $x=\sum_i x_ie_i$. Then $\langle x,B(y)\rangle_X=\sum_i x_i\overline{\langle y,Ae_i\rangle_Y}=\sum_i x_i\langle Ae_i,y\rangle_Y=\langle Ax,y\rangle_Y$. Thus $B$ is an adjoint and establishes existence without assuming the result. If $B$ and $C$ both satisfy the defining identity, $\langle x,(B-C)y\rangle=0$ for all $x,y$. Taking $x=(B-C)y$ gives $\|(B-C)y\|^2=0$, so $(B-C)y=0$ for every $y$. Hence $B=C$ and the adjoint is unique. For any bases, not necessarily orthonormal, the identity on every basis pair extends to all vectors. Indeed, if $x=\sum_i\alpha_i e_i$ and $y=\sum_j\beta_j f_j$, then $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\overline{\beta_j}\langle Ae_i,f_j\rangle$. Replacing each basis-pair term by $\langle e_i,Bf_j\rangle$ gives $\langle x,By\rangle$. The conjugate on $\beta_j$ must be kept. For orthonormal bases, $[A]_{ji}=\langle Ae_i,f_j\rangle$. The $(i,j)$ entry of $[A^*]$ is $\langle A^*f_j,e_i\rangle=\langle f_j,Ae_i\rangle=\overline{[A]_{ji}}$. This proves the conjugate-transpose formula with both bases and directions specified. Uniqueness also proves $(BA)^*=A^*B^*$, $(A^*)^*=A$, and $(\lambda A)^*=\overline\lambda A^*$. For example, $\langle BAx,z\rangle=\langle Ax,B^*z\rangle=\langle x,A^*B^*z\rangle$. The scalar formula follows because moving a scalar into the second slot conjugates it.
pitfall: The map A* is linear in y. The operation sending A to A* is conjugate-linear over C. These are different statements.
prompt: Read both map types, then test a basis pair before extending by sesquilinearity.

practice.question: When does the coordinate formula $[A^*]=[A]^\dagger$ apply directly?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: When both declared bases are orthonormal. The adjoint always exists here, but arbitrary coordinate bases require their Gram matrices.

practice.question: For $A(x_1,x_2)=2x_1+ix_2$, what is $A^*y$?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $(2y,-iy)$. Conjugate transpose reverses the rectangular matrix and conjugates its imaginary entry.

practice.question: Why does equality on every basis pair prove the adjoint identity for all x,y?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: Both sides expand with coefficients $\alpha_i\overline{\beta_j}$. Sesquilinearity gives the same coefficient expansion on both sides. Omitting conjugation would change the argument.

worked.title: A Euclidean projection with a nonsymmetric coordinate matrix
steps: In $\mathbb R^2$, take $e_1=(1,0)$ and $e_2=(1,1)$. The Euclidean projection $P(x,y)=(x,0)$ has matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ because $Pe_1=e_1$ and $Pe_2=e_1$.
The Gram matrix is $G=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $G^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$. Compute $M^TG=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, then $G^{-1}M^TG=M$.
Thus $[P^*]=M$ and $P^*=P$, while $M^T\ne M$. Self-adjointness is a property of the operator and inner product, not ordinary matrix symmetry in every basis.

objective: Derive and use the two-Gram-matrix adjoint formula without confusing coordinates with vectors.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the declared objects and relationships. It is not an algebraic solver or a general-proof animation.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on columns. Inner products are linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second.
intuition: Transpose reverses a coordinate map. The source and target metrics convert that reversal into the actual adjoint.
explanation: Let $e=(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ and $f=(f_1,\ldots,f_m)$ be arbitrary bases of inner-product spaces $X,Y$. The coordinate maps are $E:\mathbb F^n\to X$, $Ea=\sum_i a_ie_i$, and $F:\mathbb F^m\to Y$. Define $(G_X)_{ij}=\langle e_j,e_i\rangle_X$ and $(G_Y)_{ij}=\langle f_j,f_i\rangle_Y$. Then $\langle Ea,Eb\rangle=b^\dagger G_Xa$. Both Gram matrices are Hermitian positive definite, hence invertible. The coordinate identity for the adjoint is $b^\dagger G_YMa=b^\dagger N^\dagger G_Xa$. Therefore $G_YM=N^\dagger G_X$, which yields the formula below. The formula allows rectangular $M$ and different metrics on source and target.
proof: Expand $\langle Ea,Eb\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_j\overline{b_i}\langle e_j,e_i\rangle=b^\dagger G_Xa$. Conjugate symmetry gives $G_X^\dagger=G_X$. For nonzero $a$, $Ea\ne0$ because $e$ is a basis, so $a^\dagger G_Xa=\|Ea\|^2>0$. Thus $G_X$ is positive definite and invertible. The same holds for $G_Y$. For $A:X\to Y$, its coordinate matrix is $M=F^{-1}AE$. For the adjoint the domain and codomain reverse, so $N=E^{-1}A^*F$. Evaluating the defining identity on $Ea$ and $Fb$ gives $\langle FMa,Fb\rangle_Y=\langle Ea,ENb\rangle_X$. The left side is $b^\dagger G_YMa$ and the right side is $b^\dagger N^\dagger G_Xa$. The equality holds for all $a$ and $b$. Testing standard coordinate basis columns proves $G_YM=N^\dagger G_X$. Taking conjugate transposes gives $M^\dagger G_Y=G_XN$, since both Gram matrices are Hermitian. Multiplying by $G_X^{-1}$ gives $N=G_X^{-1}M^\dagger G_Y$. Conversely, define $N=G_X^{-1}M^\dagger G_Y$ and the linear map $B=ENF^{-1}:Y\to X$. Substitution in the two coordinate pairings proves $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,By\rangle$ for every $x,y$. Uniqueness of adjoints identifies $B=A^*$. The formula is a characterization, not just a necessary matrix relation. Under a source basis change $E^{\prime}=EC$ and a target basis change $F^{\prime}=FD$, the matrices become $M^{\prime}=D^{-1}MC$, $G_X^{\prime}=C^\dagger G_XC$ and $G_Y^{\prime}=D^\dagger G_YD$. Substituting these into the formula gives $N^{\prime}=C^{-1}ND$, exactly the reversed coordinate change for the same map $A^*$. This is a direct consistency calculation about declared coordinate maps.
pitfall: The Gram matrix convention is explicit. With linear-first inner products, $(G_X)_{ij}=\langle e_j,e_i\rangle$. Substituting $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle$ without transposing changes complex formulas.
prompt: Compute both Gram matrices before taking a transpose.

edges: Gram matrix supplies the inner product

practice.question: Why are $G_X$ and $G_Y$ invertible?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: The forms are positive definite and the listed vectors are bases. A nonzero coordinate column represents a nonzero vector and has strictly positive squared norm under the Gram form.

practice.question: In the nonorthonormal projection example, what is $[P^*]$?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $G^{-1}M^TG=M$. The explicit multiplication gives $M$, consistent with the basis-independent fact $P^*=P$.

practice.question: For arbitrary bases of $X,Y$, which matrix has the correct type for the adjoint?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $G_X^{-1}M^\dagger G_Y$, an $n$ by $m$ matrix. The source metric of $A$ appears on the left after inversion, and the target metric appears on the right. Dimensions also enforce the order.

worked.title: S3 restricted to a transposition subgroup
steps: Let $H=\langle(12)\rangle$. Use $H$ coordinates $(f(1),f((12)))=(a,b)$ and $S_3$ coordinates on identity, transpositions and 3-cycles. Restriction has matrix $R=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
The Gram matrices are $D_H=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/2)$ and $D_G=\operatorname{diag}(1/6,1/2,1/3)$. Consequently $D_G^{-1}R^TD_H=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$.

Induction sends $(a,b)$ to $(3a,b,0)$. In particular the nontrivial $H$ character $(1,-1)$ induces the character $(3,-1,0)$. The inner-product identity can be checked directly as $(3a\overline x)/6+(b\overline y)/2=(a\overline x+b\overline y)/2$.

objective: Prove weighted class-function adjointness and compute its coordinate matrix and regular-module example.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the declared objects and relationships. It is not an algebraic solver or a general-proof animation.
conventions: Group actions are left actions. Matrices act on columns. Inner products are linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second.
intuition: The induced-function average counts each subgroup input once for each group conjugator. The normalization cancels the group count and leaves exactly the subgroup inner product.
definition: (\operatorname{Ind}_H^G f)(g)=\frac1{|H|}\sum_{x\in G,\ x^{-1}gx\in H}f(x^{-1}gx),\qquad\langle f,F\rangle_G=\frac1{|G|}\sum_g f(g)\overline{F(g)}
explanation: For a finite group $G$, let $\mathrm{CF}(G)$ be the complex vector space of functions constant on conjugacy classes. Use the linear-first inner product $\langle f,F\rangle_G=|G|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}f(g)\overline{F(g)}$. For $H\le G$, restriction has type $\mathrm{CF}(G)\to\mathrm{CF}(H)$ and induction has the reverse type. Class indicators are function coordinates, not group-algebra basis vectors. In the indicator basis, the Gram matrix has diagonal entries $|C|/|G|$. Induction is the adjoint of restriction in one direction, and restriction is the adjoint of induction in the other. These are linear operators between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces.
proof: Restriction of a $G$-class function is an $H$-class function because $H$-conjugacy is a special case of $G$-conjugacy. Induction is a class function on $G$. Replacing $g$ by $ygy^{-1}$ and the summation variable $x$ by $yx$ gives exactly the same summands and the same membership condition. Both maps are complex-linear. The weighted form is Hermitian and positive definite. Indeed $\langle f,f\rangle_G=|G|^{-1}\sum_g|f(g)|^2$, which vanishes only for the zero function. Thus adjoints exist and are unique by the finite-dimensional adjoint theorem. Expand $\langle\operatorname{Ind}f,F\rangle_G=(|G||H|)^{-1}\sum_{g\in G}\sum_{x:\,x^{-1}gx\in H}f(x^{-1}gx)\overline{F(g)}$. The change of variables $h=x^{-1}gx$ is a bijection between the summation pairs $(g,x)$ and $(h,x)\in H\times G$, with inverse $g=xhx^{-1}$. Since $F$ is a class function, $F(xhx^{-1})=F(h)$. Therefore the sum becomes $(|G||H|)^{-1}\sum_{x\in G}\sum_{h\in H}f(h)\overline{F(h)}=|H|^{-1}\sum_{h\in H}f(h)\overline{F(h)}=\langle f,\operatorname{Res}F\rangle_H$. This proves the adjoint identity for all class functions, without first restricting to characters. Uniqueness follows directly too. If $B$ also satisfies the identity, then $\langle f,(B-\operatorname{Res})F\rangle_H=0$ for all $f,F$. Set $f=(B-\operatorname{Res})F$ to conclude $B=\operatorname{Res}$. Taking adjoints once more gives $\operatorname{Res}^*=\operatorname{Ind}$. For a class $C$, the indicator $\delta_C$ equals one on $C$ and zero elsewhere. Distinct indicators are orthogonal, and their squared norms are $|C|/|G|$. Thus the indicator-basis Gram matrix is $D_G=\operatorname{diag}(|C|/|G|)$. If $R$ is the matrix of restriction, the matrix of induction is $D_G^{-1}R^\dagger D_H$. This is the arbitrary-basis adjoint formula with the two spaces reversed.
pitfall: An unweighted dot product on conjugacy-class values changes the adjoint. Class sizes and group orders are part of the definition.
prompt: Track the factor $1/(|G||H|)$ before changing variables in the double sum.

practice.question: Which inner product makes the stated adjoint identity true?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $|G|^{-1}\sum_g f(g)\overline{F(g)}$. The proof cancels the number of conjugators using group-order normalization. In class coordinates this gives class-size weights.

practice.question: For $H=\langle(12)\rangle\le S_3$, what is Ind of $(a,b)$ in the stated class coordinates?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $(3a,b,0)$. The diagonal class weights give the displayed matrix, and no 3-cycle is conjugate into H.

practice.question: What multiplicity does an irreducible of degree d have in the complex regular module?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: d. Adjointness with induction from the identity gives inner product $\chi(1)=d$. The dimension contribution is then $d^2$.

worked.title: Curry an explicit finite function
steps: Then $\widehat h(0)$ is the function $a\mapsto2,b\mapsto5$, while $\widehat h(1)$ is $a\mapsto7,b\mapsto11$. Evaluating these functions recovers all four original values.
If $\alpha$ swaps 0 and 1 and $\beta(n)=n+1$, either naturality route gives at $(0,a)$ the value $\beta(h(1,a))=8$. This is an explicit map-level check.

objective: Distinguish objects, morphisms and functors, then verify a typed natural Hom-set bijection.
labScope: The diagram shows the types of the declared maps. It illustrates the correspondence and does not compute a universal property.
conventions: All modules are unital left modules unless a right action is specified. Matrices act on columns. No commutation of noncommutative ring elements is assumed.
intuition: Currying replaces a function of a pair by a function whose values are functions. The same translation works before or after changing an input or output map.
explanation: A category has objects, sets $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(X,Y)$ of morphisms with source and target, identity morphisms, and associative composition. In $R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$ the objects are unital left $R$-modules and morphisms are $R$-linear maps. A functor $F:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$ assigns both objects and morphisms, preserving sources, targets, identities and composition. Naturality means compatibility with every source precomposition and target postcomposition, not a separate arbitrary bijection for every object pair. In the set example, fix a set $A$. Take $F(X)=X\times A$ and $U(Y)=Y^A$, the set of functions $A\to Y$. Currying is the natural bijection $h\mapsto[x\mapsto(a\mapsto h(x,a))]$.
proof: Composition of $R$-linear maps is $R$-linear, identity maps are $R$-linear, and ordinary function composition is associative. Thus unital left modules and their linear maps form the category $R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}$. In any category, identities are unique because two proposed identities compose to each other in both orders. For a fixed set $A$, define $F(\alpha):X^{\prime}\times A\to X\times A$ by $(x^{\prime},a)\mapsto(\alpha(x^{\prime}),a)$. Define $U(\beta):Y^A\to Y^{\prime A}$ by $f\mapsto\beta\circ f$. Substituting a pair or a function proves that both operations preserve identities and composition. Hence $F$ and $U$ are functors, not just formulas on objects. For $h:X\times A\to Y$, define $\widehat h:X\to Y^A$ by $\widehat h(x)(a)=h(x,a)$. For $f:X\to Y^A$, define $\check f:X\times A\to Y$ by $\check f(x,a)=f(x)(a)$. Every output has the declared type. Evaluation gives $\check{\widehat h}(x,a)=h(x,a)$ and $\widehat{\check f}(x)(a)=f(x)(a)$ for all inputs. Thus these operations are inverse bijections. For $\alpha:X^{\prime}\to X$ and $\beta:Y\to Y^{\prime}$, both currying routes evaluate at $(x^{\prime},a)$ to $\beta(h(\alpha(x^{\prime}),a))$. Hence $\widehat{\beta\circ h\circ(\alpha\times1_A)}=U(\beta)\circ\widehat h\circ\alpha$. This is naturality in both variables. The source arrow reverses its effect on the Hom set because it acts by precomposition. The abstract definition replaces these two set-valued Hom constructions by $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D}(F(-),-)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(-,U(-))$. An adjunction is a specified natural bijection between them. No inner product is part of this definition. The next lesson verifies an analogous correspondence with linearity and balancing built into its types.
pitfall: Objects are not morphisms, and a functor is not merely an object formula. A Hom-set bijection need not be linear, and currying of arbitrary set functions does not itself prove a module tensor-Hom theorem.
prompt: Name the source and target of each function before currying it.

practice.question: What makes a family of Hom-set bijections an adjunction?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: Naturality in both source and target. Precomposition and postcomposition must commute with the chosen correspondence.

practice.question: For the finite h in the example, what is $\widehat h(1)(b)$?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: 11. Currying preserves the value at the pair $(1,b)$.

practice.question: For $\alpha:X^{\prime}\to X$, which direction is induced on $\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)$?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: Precomposition gives $\operatorname{Hom}(X,Y)\to\operatorname{Hom}(X^{\prime},Y)$. The composite $h\circ\alpha$ has source $X^{\prime}$ and target $Y$. This is contravariance in the first variable.

worked.title: The regular bimodule reduces the correspondence to evaluation
steps: Take $S=R=A$, with $M=A$ as its regular bimodule. The map $A\otimes_AV\to V$, $a\otimes v\mapsto av$, has inverse $v\mapsto1\otimes v$. Balancing and $a\otimes v=1\otimes av$ prove the two identities.

For a left $A$-module $W$, evaluation $\operatorname{Hom}_A(A,W)\to W$ sends $f$ to $f(1)$, with inverse $w\mapsto[a\mapsto aw]$. The Hom $A$-action satisfies $(bf)(1)=f(b)=bf(1)$, so this is an $A$-module isomorphism.
Under these identifications, tensor-Hom becomes the identity correspondence on $\operatorname{Hom}_A(V,W)$. This also checks the action when $A$ is noncommutative.

objective: Construct both directions of the left-module tensor-Hom correspondence and verify every linearity and balancing condition.
labScope: The diagram shows the types of the declared maps. It illustrates the correspondence and does not compute a universal property.
conventions: All modules are unital left modules unless a right action is specified. Matrices act on columns. No commutation of noncommutative ring elements is assumed.
intuition: A map on a tensor can be read one input at a time. The outer map is R-linear exactly when its evaluations satisfy the relation that balances the tensor.
explanation: Let $S,R$ be associative unital rings and ${}_SM_R$ a unital bimodule, so $(sm)r=s(mr)$. Let $V$ be a unital left $R$-module and $W$ a unital left $S$-module. Give $M\otimes_RV$ its left $S$-action $s(m\otimes v)=sm\otimes v$. Give $\operatorname{Hom}_S(M,W)$ the left $R$-action $(rf)(m)=f(mr)$. There are two levels of linearity. For each $v$, $\widehat T(v)$ must be $S$-linear in $m$. The assignment $v\mapsto\widehat T(v)$ must be $R$-linear into that Hom module. The correspondence is an isomorphism of abelian groups for general rings. It is linear over a common commutative central scalar ring when the algebras, bimodule and modules have compatible scalar actions.
proof: First verify the actions. The left $S$-action on $M\otimes_RV$ descends because $(sm)r\otimes v=sm\otimes rv$, using bimodule compatibility. For $f\in\operatorname{Hom}_S(M,W)$, the function $rf$ is $S$-linear because $(rf)(sm)=f((sm)r)=f(s(mr))=s f(mr)$. It is additive in all required inputs. Further, $(r(r^{\prime}f))(m)=f((mr)r^{\prime})=f(m(rr^{\prime}))=((rr^{\prime})f)(m)$ and $1_Rf=f$. Thus the Hom space is a left $R$-module with exactly this multiplication order. Let $T:M\otimes_RV\to W$ be $S$-linear. For fixed $v$, $\widehat T(v)(m)=T(m\otimes v)$ is additive in $m$ and satisfies $\widehat T(v)(sm)=T(sm\otimes v)=sT(m\otimes v)$. Thus each output is an $S$-map. Additivity of $\widehat T$ in $v$ follows from tensor additivity. For outer $R$-linearity, compute $\widehat T(rv)(m)=T(m\otimes rv)=T(mr\otimes v)=\widehat T(v)(mr)=(r\widehat T(v))(m)$. Equality at every $m$ proves $\widehat T(rv)=r\widehat T(v)$. This checks the second level of linearity instead of conflating it with the first. Conversely, let $f:V\to\operatorname{Hom}_S(M,W)$ be $R$-linear. The function $B(m,v)=f(v)(m)$ is additive in each variable. Its balancing is $B(m,rv)=f(rv)(m)=(rf(v))(m)=f(v)(mr)=B(mr,v)$. The tensor universal property supplies a unique additive map $T_f:M\otimes_RV\to W$ with $T_f(m\otimes v)=f(v)(m)$. The map $T_f$ is $S$-linear because $T_f(sm\otimes v)=f(v)(sm)=s f(v)(m)=sT_f(m\otimes v)$, and pure tensors generate the tensor product additively. Both inverse identities are explicit. For every $v,m$, $\widehat{T_f}(v)(m)=f(v)(m)$, and for every pure tensor, $T_{\widehat T}(m\otimes v)=T(m\otimes v)$. Thus the constructions are inverse. Addition is preserved by evaluation, so the outer correspondence is an isomorphism of abelian groups. If all data are modules over a common commutative ring $k$ with compatible central actions, multiplying $T$ by $c\in k$ gives $\widehat{cT}(v)(m)=c\widehat T(v)(m)$. The correspondence is then $k$-linear. No such scalar claim is made for an arbitrary noncommutative $R$.
pitfall: The formula $(rf)(m)=f(mr)$ uses the right R-action on M. Replacing it by an unavailable left R-action is a typing error. General noncommutative Hom sets need not carry an outer R-module structure.
prompt: Check the Hom action, then check inner S-linearity, outer R-linearity and reverse balancing in that order.

practice.question: At what level of linearity is the general-ring correspondence always valid?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: As an isomorphism of abelian groups. The Hom spaces have addition. A common central scalar ring supplies a stronger linearity statement when compatible structure is declared.

practice.question: For $M=\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$, what determines a map $M\to W$?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: An element $w\in W$ with $nw=0$. The image of the generator must respect $n\overline1=0$, which is precisely the annihilator condition.

practice.question: Which equality permits the reverse map to descend?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $f(rv)(m)=f(v)(mr)$. Outer R-linearity with the declared Hom action gives the balancing relation $B(m,rv)=B(mr,v)$.

worked.title: Naturality with two explicit linear maps
steps: Take $R=S=M=\mathbb C$, $V=V^{\prime}=W=W^{\prime}=\mathbb C$. Let $T(m\otimes v)=3mv$, $\alpha(v^{\prime})=2v^{\prime}$ and $\beta(w)=5w$.

The source-precompose and target-postcompose map is $m\otimes v^{\prime}\mapsto30mv^{\prime}$. Currying first gives $\widehat T(v)(m)=3mv$, and then applying $\alpha$ and $U\beta$ also gives $30mv^{\prime}$. The equality uses the correct source direction.

objective: Prove naturality in both variables, compute unit and counit, and distinguish adjunction from inverse functors.
labScope: The diagram shows the types of the declared maps. It illustrates the correspondence and does not compute a universal property.
conventions: All modules are unital left modules unless a right action is specified. Matrices act on columns. No commutation of noncommutative ring elements is assumed.
intuition: Every route around naturality evaluates to the same expression. Unit and counit are the two special cases obtained from identity maps.
explanation: With ${}_SM_R$ fixed, set $F(V)=M\otimes_RV$ and $U(W)=\operatorname{Hom}_S(M,W)$. For an $R$-map $\alpha:V^{\prime}\to V$, define $F\alpha=1_M\otimes\alpha$. For an $S$-map $\beta:W\to W^{\prime}$, define $(U\beta)(f)=\beta\circ f$. The tensor-Hom isomorphism sends $T$ to $\widehat T$ as in the preceding lesson. The unit has type $V\to U(FV)$ and the counit has type $F(UW)\to W$. They satisfy triangle identities, but need not be isomorphisms. Naturality here concerns explicitly declared source and target module maps.
proof: The map $1_M\otimes\alpha$ is well-defined because $mr\otimes\alpha(v)=m\otimes r\alpha(v)=m\otimes\alpha(rv)$. It is $S$-linear by the left action on $M$. Postcomposition by $\beta$ preserves $S$-linearity and the Hom $R$-action, because $\beta(f(mr))=(r(\beta f))(m)$. Evaluation on pure tensors or functions verifies identities and composition, so $F$ and $U$ are functors. For $T:F(V)\to W$, $v^{\prime}\in V^{\prime}$ and $m\in M$, the left side of naturality evaluates to $\beta(T(m\otimes\alpha(v^{\prime})))$. The right side evaluates to $(U\beta)(\widehat T(\alpha(v^{\prime})))(m)$, which is the same expression. Equality at every $m$ and $v^{\prime}$ proves naturality simultaneously in source and target. The identity map of $FV$ corresponds to $\eta_V:V\to U(FV)$ with $\eta_V(v)(m)=m\otimes v$. Each output is $S$-linear in $m$, and $\eta_V(rv)(m)=m\otimes rv=mr\otimes v=(r\eta_V(v))(m)$ proves $R$-linearity. The identity map of $UW$ corresponds in reverse to $\varepsilon_W:F(UW)\to W$, $m\otimes f\mapsto f(m)$. Its balancing is $(rf)(m)=f(mr)$ and its $S$-linearity follows from that of $f$. For a pure tensor $m\otimes v\in FV$, applying $F\eta_V$ gives $m\otimes\eta_V(v)$, and applying $\varepsilon_{FV}$ gives $\eta_V(v)(m)=m\otimes v$. Pure tensors generate, so the first triangle identity follows. For $f\in UW$, $\eta_{UW}(f)$ sends $m$ to $m\otimes f$. Postcomposing with $\varepsilon_W$ sends that output to $f(m)$ for every $m$, giving the second triangle identity. For an original concrete failure of inverse functors, take $S=R=\mathbb C$ and $M=\mathbb C^2$. Then $F(\mathbb C)=\mathbb C^2$ and $U(F(\mathbb C))=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb C^2)$ has dimension four. The unit sends $z$ to $zI_M$, a one-dimensional subspace. It is not surjective, so these adjoint functors are not inverse equivalences. Induction-restriction is the specialization $S=\mathbb CG$, $R=\mathbb CH$, $M=\mathbb CG$. Evaluation $E_W:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb CG}(\mathbb CG,W)\to\operatorname{Res}_H^GW$ sends $f$ to $f(1)$. Its inverse sends $w$ to the $\mathbb CG$-linear function $b\mapsto bw$. The inverse assignment is $\mathbb CH$-linear, since $(hf)(1)=f(h)=hf(1)$. Thus the adjunction becomes $T\mapsto[v\mapsto T(1\otimes v)]$ and $\phi\mapsto[b\otimes v\mapsto b\phi(v)]$.
pitfall: The arrows in naturality have fixed directions. Precomposition uses V-prime to V, while postcomposition uses W to W-prime. Triangle identities do not imply that every unit or counit is invertible.
prompt: Evaluate both sides at one vector and one bimodule element. Then inspect the types of the unit and counit.

practice.question: What extra conclusion is not supplied by adjunction alone?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: Invertibility of all units and counits. An equivalence needs invertibility. The dimension example shows that an adjunction alone need not supply it.

practice.question: In the scalar naturality example, what is the coefficient after applying $\alpha=2$, $T=3$ and $\beta=5$?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: 30. Both routes give $5\cdot3\cdot2=30$ and preserve the input types.

practice.question: How does $U\varepsilon_W\circ\eta_{UW}$ act on $f$ at $m$?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: It sends $f$ to the function $m\mapsto\varepsilon_W(m\otimes f)=f(m)$. Evaluation proves the second triangle identity directly, without a basis.

source.title: Iain W. Stewart, MIT 8.09 Advanced Classical Mechanics
source.section: Chapter 3, quadratic small oscillations and generalized normal modes, Sections 3.1-3.2

subject: Representations & symmetry

worked.title: One edge and one transverse-looking displacement
steps: For the edge joining $r_1$ to $r_2$, $n_{12}=(0,1,1)/\sqrt2$. If $u_1=(0,q,0)$ and $u_2=0$, its first-order extension is $q/\sqrt2$.

This edge contributes $kq^2/4$ to the potential. Its linear force on mass 1 is $-k(q/\sqrt2)n_{12}=(0,-kq/2,-kq/2)$. A displacement along one coordinate can therefore induce force in two coordinates. This is one edge contribution, not the total force from all six springs.

proofStatus: Complete proof for the stated ideal model here
objective: State the exact mechanical assumptions and derive the quadratic stiffness and generalized mode equation.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the objects and equations. It is not a spring simulation, a force solver or experimental validation. Exact algebra is developed in the lesson.
conventions: Real three-dimensional column displacements and left orthogonal group actions are used. Character decompositions use complexification of these real representations. The spring model is free, unstressed, central and linearized at the declared regular tetrahedron.
intuition: A central spring senses only the component of relative displacement along its equilibrium edge at first order. Six such linear extension measurements determine the quadratic energy.
explanation: Four identical point masses $m>0$ have equilibrium positions $r_1=a(1,1,1)$, $r_2=a(1,-1,-1)$, $r_3=a(-1,1,-1)$ and $r_4=a(-1,-1,1)$, where $a>0$. Every pair is joined by one massless central Hooke spring with stiffness $k>0$ and rest length $\ell_0=2\sqrt2a$. There are six springs, all unstressed at equilibrium. The frame is free in three-dimensional space, with no anchors, central mass, angular forces, damping, prestress or external potential. The displacement is $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_4)\in(\mathbb R^3)^4$. For $d_{ij}=r_i-r_j$ and $n_{ij}=d_{ij}/\ell_0$, the first-order extension is $e_{ij}=n_{ij}\cdot(u_i-u_j)$. The harmonic potential is $V_2(u)=\frac{k}{2}\sum_{i<j}e_{ij}^2=\frac12u^TKu$. The stiffness $K$ is positive semidefinite. The mass matrix in the twelve Cartesian coordinates is $M=mI_{12}$.
theorem: M\ddot u+Ku=0,\qquad Kf=\omega^2Mf,\qquad K_{ii}=k\sum_{j\ne i}n_{ij}n_{ij}^T,\quad K_{ij}=-kn_{ij}n_{ij}^T
proof: Every equilibrium difference has two nonzero coordinates of magnitude $2a$, so every edge has length $2\sqrt2a$. For a nonzero vector $d$, differentiating the norm gives $\|d+v\|=\|d\|+(d/\|d\|)\cdot v+O(\|v\|^2)$. Therefore the extension of edge $ij$ is $e_{ij}+O(\|u\|^2)$ with $e_{ij}=n_{ij}\cdot(u_i-u_j)$. Because the springs are unstressed, the extension has zero constant term. Squaring gives the quadratic potential $V_2=\frac{k}{2}\sum e_{ij}^2$, and $V_{\mathrm{exact}}=V_2+O(\|u\|^3)$ near zero. Prestress would introduce an additional quadratic contribution from the second derivative of edge length, which is why the zero-prestress assumption matters. The contribution of one edge to the force on mass $i$ is $-k n_{ij}n_{ij}^T(u_i-u_j)$, while the force on mass $j$ is its negative. Thus the diagonal stiffness blocks receive $k n_{ij}n_{ij}^T$ and the off-diagonal blocks receive $-k n_{ij}n_{ij}^T$. This proves the displayed block formula and the symmetry $K^T=K$. Each term $\frac{k}{2}e_{ij}^2$ is nonnegative, so $K$ is positive semidefinite. The kinetic energy is exactly $\frac12\dot u^TM\dot u$ with $M=mI_{12}$. Euler-Lagrange differentiation of $T-V_2$ gives $M\ddot u+Ku=0$. Substituting $u(t)=f\cos(\omega t)$ gives $Kf=\omega^2Mf$. Zero eigenvalues correspond to free linearized motions rather than positive-frequency vibrations. For a translation $u_i=c$, every relative displacement is zero. For an infinitesimal rotation $u_i=\Omega r_i$ with $\Omega^T=-\Omega$, the extension is $n_{ij}\cdot\Omega d_{ij}=\ell_0^{-1}d_{ij}^T\Omega d_{ij}=0$. These six rigid-motion directions are in the kernel. A later lesson proves there are no additional zero directions in this particular fully braced tetrahedron.
pitfall: The exact spring potential is nonlinear in Cartesian displacements. Its quadratic approximation is the small-oscillation model. Symmetry of the equilibrium does not supply a force law or remove prestress terms from a different model.
prompt: Follow one edge extension to its energy, then differentiate the full quadratic energy.

edges: square and sum the central extensions
differentiate and use harmonic time dependence

practice.question: Which assumption justifies using only squared first-order extensions for the quadratic potential?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: Every spring is unstressed at the equilibrium. Zero extension at equilibrium removes the product of a nonzero constant extension with the second-order length change.

practice.question: For $n=(0,1,1)/\sqrt2$ and relative displacement $(0,q,0)$, what is the edge energy to quadratic order?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $kq^2/4$. The extension is $q/\sqrt2$, and the energy is $k e^2/2=kq^2/4$.

practice.question: What is the correct normal-mode equation with a general positive mass matrix?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $Kf=\omega^2Mf$. Harmonic substitution in $M\ddot u+Ku=0$ produces the generalized eigenvalue equation.

title: The full tetrahedral displacement representation

subject: Representations & symmetry

worked.title: A reflection fixes two sites but has displacement trace two
steps: The matrix $R(x,y,z)=(x,z,y)$ fixes $r_1$ and $r_2$ and exchanges $r_3,r_4$. It is a reflection, with determinant $-1$ and vector trace one.

The two fixed sites each contribute trace one, so the twelve-dimensional displacement trace is two. Counting fixed sites alone happens to give the same value here only because the vector trace is one.

proofStatus: Complete proof for the stated ideal model here
objective: Construct the full Td action, derive all five character rows and decompose the twelve-dimensional displacement character.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the objects and equations. It is not a spring simulation, a force solver or experimental validation. Exact algebra is developed in the lesson.
conventions: Real three-dimensional column displacements and left orthogonal group actions are used. Character decompositions use complexification of these real representations. The spring model is free, unstressed, central and linearized at the declared regular tetrahedron.
intuition: The site label moves and the attached three-vector transforms. Their traces multiply because displacement space is the tensor product of the site module and the polar vector module.
explanation: Let $G=T_d$ be the full orthogonal symmetry group of the four equilibrium vertices, including improper symmetries. A symmetry is an orthogonal matrix $R_g$ together with its induced permutation $p_g\in S_4$, where $R_gr_i=r_{p_g(i)}$. On displacement columns, $(D(g)u)_{p_g(i)}=R_gu_i$, or equivalently $(D(g)u)_j=R_gu_{p_g^{-1}(j)}$. Use the class order $1,(123),(12)(34),(1234),(12)$, with sizes $1,8,3,6,6$. In physical notation these are $1,8C_3,3C_2,6S_4,6\sigma_d$. The five rows are $A_1=(1,1,1,1,1)$, $A_2=(1,1,1,-1,-1)$, $E=(2,-1,2,0,0)$, $T_1=(3,0,-1,1,-1)$ and $T_2=(3,0,-1,-1,1)$. Here $T_2$ is the polar vector representation and $T_1$ is its sign twist.
proof: The vertex identities are $\sum_i r_i=0$ and $\sum_i r_ir_i^T=4a^2I$, with $r_i\cdot r_i=3a^2$ and $r_i\cdot r_j=-a^2$ for $i\ne j$. For any permutation $p\in S_4$, define $R_p=(4a^2)^{-1}\sum_i r_{p(i)}r_i^T$. Multiplying by $r_j$ gives $R_pr_j=r_{p(j)}$. These vertices span $\mathbb R^3$ and their inner products are preserved, so $R_p$ is orthogonal. The matrix is unique on the spanning set, and $R_pR_q=R_{pq}$. Thus every permutation gives a unique symmetry and $T_d\cong S_4$. The site permutation module $P=\mathbb R^4$ maps onto the polar vector module $V=\mathbb R^3$ by $e_i\mapsto r_i$. Its kernel is the one-dimensional all-ones line, and its zero-sum complement maps isomorphically to $V$. Therefore $\chi_V=\chi_P-1$. The fixed-site counts in the declared class order are $(4,1,0,0,2)$, giving $\chi_V=(3,0,-1,-1,1)$. The determinant of the four-site permutation action is sign, while its trivial line has determinant one, so $\det R_p=\operatorname{sgn}(p)$. The action on displacements is $D(g)=P(g)\otimes R_g$. This formula verifies the group law directly and gives $\chi_D=\chi_P\chi_V=(12,0,0,0,2)$. Equivalently, a moved site gives an off-diagonal three-by-three block and contributes zero to trace. A fixed site contributes $\operatorname{tr}R_g$. Construct the character rows instead of assuming them. Trivial and sign give $A_1$ and $A_2$. The zero-sum site module gives $T_2$ and its sign twist gives $T_1$. For $E$, let $S_4$ permute the three partitions of four labels into two unordered pairs. Their fixed counts are $(3,0,3,1,1)$, and removing the invariant all-ones line gives $(2,-1,2,0,0)$. Thus every displayed row is an actual representation character. The weighted norm of $T_2$ is $(9+3+6+6)/24=1$, and twisting by sign preserves this norm. The weighted norm of $E$ is $(4+8+12)/24=1$. Trivial and sign also have norm one. Hence all five are complex irreducible, their distinct rows make them pairwise nonisomorphic, and $1^2+1^2+2^2+3^2+3^2=24$ proves completeness. They have the explicit real models just constructed. Weighted inner products with $\chi_D$ give multiplicities $(12+12)/24=1$ for $A_1$, $(12-12)/24=0$ for $A_2$, $24/24=1$ for $E$, $(36-12)/24=1$ for $T_1$, and $(36+12)/24=2$ for $T_2$. Their dimensions sum to $1+2+3+6=12$. This is a symmetry decomposition, and does not yet supply frequencies.
pitfall: The full group has order 24. The proper rotation subgroup has order 12 and is $A_4$. Using only proper rotations loses the distinction between polar and axial three-vectors.
prompt: Multiply the number of fixed sites by the vector trace in the stated class order.

edges: transform the vector attached to the site

practice.question: Which symmetry group distinguishes T1 from T2 in this model?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: The full orthogonal tetrahedral group of order 24. The rows differ on improper classes. On proper rotations the polar and axial vector actions agree.

practice.question: What is the displacement trace for a symmetry fixing one vertex with vector trace zero?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: 0. The trace is the fixed-site count times the vector trace.

practice.question: What is the irreducible decomposition of D in the stated convention?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $A_1\oplus E\oplus T_1\oplus2T_2$. Weighted inner products with the five constructed rows give multiplicities $1,0,1,1,2$ and total dimension twelve.

subject: Representations & symmetry

worked.title: Move only one vertex
steps: Let $u_1=b$ and $u_2=u_3=u_4=0$. The inverse formulas give $c=b/4$ and $A=br_1^T/(4a^2)$.
At $r_1$, $Ar_1=3b/4$, while at each other vertex $Ar_j=-b/4$. Adding $c$ recovers exactly the original four displacements. This arbitrary localized motion is included in the affine coordinates.

proofStatus: Complete proof for the stated ideal model here
objective: Recover unique affine coordinates, derive their mass metric and identify symmetric and exterior square spaces.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the objects and equations. It is not a spring simulation, a force solver or experimental validation. Exact algebra is developed in the lesson.
conventions: Real three-dimensional column displacements and left orthogonal group actions are used. Character decompositions use complexification of these real representations. The spring model is free, unstressed, central and linearized at the declared regular tetrahedron.
intuition: The vertex sum isolates translation, and the second moment isolates the matrix. The mass metric then separates translation, skew matrices and symmetric matrices orthogonally.
definition: c=\frac14\sum_i u_i,\qquad A=\frac1{4a^2}\sum_i u_ir_i^T,\qquad A=\Omega+S,\ \Omega^T=-\Omega,\ S^T=S
explanation: Use the same four vertices $r_i$ and write any displacement as $u_i=c+Ar_i$, where $c\in\mathbb R^3$ and $A\in M_3(\mathbb R)$. These are coordinates for arbitrary small displacement data, not an assumption that the body remains rigid or that deformation is globally affine away from the four masses. The mass inner product is $\langle u,v\rangle_M=m\sum_i u_i\cdot v_i$. The affine coordinates transform as $c\mapsto R_gc$ and $A\mapsto R_gAR_g^{-1}$. In these coordinates, $\langle(c,A),(d,B)\rangle_M=4m\,c\cdot d+4ma^2\operatorname{tr}(A^TB)$. Orthogonality identifies $\operatorname{End}(V)$ with $V\otimes V$, with symmetric matrices representing $\operatorname{Sym}^2V$ and skew matrices representing $\bigwedge^2V$.
theorem: (\mathbb R^3)^4\cong\mathbb R^3\oplus M_3(\mathbb R),\qquad T=2m\|\dot c\|^2+2ma^2\operatorname{tr}(\dot A^T\dot A)
proof: The vertices satisfy $\sum_i r_i=0$ and $\sum_i r_ir_i^T=4a^2I$. If $u_i=c+Ar_i$, averaging gives $c=\frac14\sum_i u_i$. Multiplying by $r_i^T$ and summing gives $\sum_i u_ir_i^T=4a^2A$, so the stated inverse formulas are necessary. For arbitrary $u_i$, define $c,A$ by those formulas. At vertex $r_j$, $Ar_j=(4a^2)^{-1}\sum_i u_i(r_i\cdot r_j)=\frac14(3u_j-\sum_{i\ne j}u_i)=u_j-c$. Therefore $c+Ar_j=u_j$ at every vertex. The formulas are both a reconstruction and a uniqueness proof, so the affine parametrization is a linear isomorphism. Let $v_i=d+Br_i$. Expanding the mass pairing gives $m\sum_i(c+Ar_i)\cdot(d+Br_i)$. The mixed terms vanish because $\sum_i r_i=0$. The constant part is $4mc\cdot d$. The matrix part is $m\operatorname{tr}(A^TB\sum_i r_ir_i^T)=4ma^2\operatorname{tr}(A^TB)$. Applying half this norm to velocities gives the kinetic energy formula. Every $A$ has the unique decomposition $S=(A+A^T)/2$ and $\Omega=(A-A^T)/2$. The spaces have dimensions six and three. Their Frobenius pairing vanishes because $\operatorname{tr}(S^T\Omega)=\operatorname{tr}(S\Omega)=-\operatorname{tr}(S\Omega)$. Thus translation, skew and symmetric pieces are orthogonal in the mass metric. For a symmetry $R$ with vertex permutation $p$, the transformed displacement satisfies $u^{\prime}_{p(i)}=R(c+Ar_i)=Rc+RAR^{-1}r_{p(i)}$. Uniqueness of affine coordinates gives $c^{\prime}=Rc$ and $A^{\prime}=RAR^{-1}$. Orthogonality of $R$ preserves symmetric and skew matrices, as well as their mass metric. The orthogonal metric identifies $V$ with its dual, so $\operatorname{End}(V)\cong V\otimes V$ equivariantly. The interchange of tensor factors corresponds to matrix transpose. Its plus-one eigenspace is the symmetric matrices, namely $\operatorname{Sym}^2V$, and its minus-one eigenspace is the skew matrices, namely $\bigwedge^2V$. This uses the real field, where two is invertible.
pitfall: Affine coordinates are unique because the four vertices are affinely independent. The six raw entries of a symmetric matrix do not have equal masses. Off-diagonal entries occur twice in the Frobenius norm.
prompt: Recover c by averaging, recover A by the vertex second moment, then compute the mass norm.

practice.question: What makes the inverse coordinate formulas unique?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: The tetrahedron is nondegenerate with $a>0$ and has the stated vertex moments. Affine independence and the invertible second moment determine the coordinates before any force law is used.

practice.question: If only $u_1=b$ is nonzero, what is c?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $b/4$. Averaging the four displacements isolates the translation coordinate.

practice.question: What mass weight belongs to a raw symmetric off-diagonal entry?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: $8ma^2$, because it appears twice in the Frobenius norm. For $S_{12}=S_{21}=q$, the squared Frobenius norm contains $2q^2$.

worked.title: A reflection distinguishes translation from rotation
steps: Let $R(x,y,z)=(x,z,y)$, so $\det R=-1$. A translation with $c=(1,0,0)$ transforms to $Rc=c$.

A rotation with $\omega=(1,0,0)$ transforms to $\det(R)R\omega=-\omega$. The same reflection therefore has eigenvalue plus one on this translation parameter and minus one on this rotation parameter. Polar and axial behavior are distinct.

proofStatus: Complete proof for the stated model and hypotheses here
objective: Prove that the kernel consists of three translations and three rotations, and identify the internal A1 plus E plus T2 space.
labScope: The diagram illustrates the mathematical decomposition and declared maps. It does not simulate motion, solve a force system or validate a real material. The exact calculation is in the teaching text.
conventions: Real column displacements and left orthogonal actions are used. Character theory uses their complexification. Polar vectors transform by R, axial vectors by det(R)R. The physical model remains free and unstressed with four equal masses and six equal central springs.
intuition: The translation vector is polar. The axis and angular-velocity parameter of a rotation is axial, so a reflection contributes an extra determinant sign.
definition: \mathcal T=\{(c)_i\},\quad\mathcal R=\{(\omega\times r_i)_i\},\quad\mathcal I=(\mathcal T\oplus\mathcal R)^{\perp_M}=\{(Sr_i)_i:S^T=S\}
explanation: In the affine coordinates $u_i=c+Ar_i$, translations have $A=0$. Infinitesimal rotations have $c=0$ and $A=\Omega$ skew-symmetric, equivalently $\Omega r=\omega\times r$. Internal strains have $c=0$ and $A=S$ symmetric. All three spaces are orthogonal for the mass inner product. With class order $1,(123),(12)(34),(1234),(12)$, translations have character $T_2=(3,0,-1,-1,1)$ and rotations have $T_1=(3,0,-1,1,-1)$. Subtracting both from $(12,0,0,0,2)$ gives internal character $(6,0,2,0,2)=A_1+E+T_2$. The six central-edge constraints show that no additional zero mode survives in the internal symmetric space.
theorem: \ker K=\mathcal T\oplus\mathcal R,\quad\dim\ker K=6,\qquad\mathcal I\cong A_1\oplus E\oplus T_2
proof: The translation space has dimension three and transforms by $c\mapsto Rc$, so it is the polar $T_2$ module. The map $\omega\mapsto(\omega\times r_i)_i$ is injective because a vector parallel to every spanning vertex must be zero. Hence rotations also have dimension three. For an orthogonal matrix $R$, $R(x\times y)=\det(R)((Rx)\times(Ry))$. This follows by pairing with $Rz$ and using the determinant definition of the scalar triple product. Thus $R(\omega\times r)=\det(R)(R\omega)\times Rr$. The transformed rotation parameter is $\det(R)R\omega$. Since $\det R$ is the permutation sign, rotations have the sign twist $T_1$ of the polar representation. The affine mass-metric calculation proves $\mathcal T$, $\mathcal R$ and the symmetric strain space are mutually orthogonal and have dimensions $3,3,6$. Translations and rotations lie in $\ker K$ because they give zero first-order edge extensions. It remains to prove that the symmetric space has no zero extension pattern. For $S=(s_{ij})$ symmetric, the six edge directions are proportional to $(1,\pm1,0)$, $(1,0,\pm1)$ and $(0,1,\pm1)$. Zero extension on the first pair gives $s_{11}+s_{22}\pm2s_{12}=0$, hence $s_{12}=0$ and $s_{11}+s_{22}=0$. The other pairs give $s_{13}=s_{23}=0$, $s_{11}+s_{33}=0$ and $s_{22}+s_{33}=0$. These three diagonal equations force all three diagonal entries zero over $\mathbb R$. Thus $S=0$. Because $V_2$ is a positive sum of extension squares, $Ku=0$ is equivalent to all six extensions vanishing. The preceding argument proves $\ker K=\mathcal T\oplus\mathcal R$. Its mass-orthogonal complement is the six-dimensional internal strain space. Its character is obtained by subtraction, giving $(6,0,2,0,2)$ and hence $A_1\oplus E\oplus T_2$. The decomposition is also explicit in matrices. Every signed coordinate permutation with product of its three coordinate signs equal to one preserves the vertex set. There are $6\cdot4=24$ such matrices, so they are all of $T_d$. Conjugation preserves the scalar line $\mathbb RI$, diagonal trace-zero matrices and off-diagonal symmetric matrices, of dimensions one, two and three. On the last space, the linear map $S\mapsto(S_{23},S_{13},S_{12})$ is an equivariant isomorphism to the polar vector module. For a diagonal sign change, the coefficient complementary to index $i$ gains the sign $\varepsilon_j\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon_i$ because $\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2\varepsilon_3=1$. A coordinate permutation permutes these complementary coefficients in the same way as vector coordinates. The scalar line is $A_1$, the last space is $T_2$, and subtracting their characters from the known internal character identifies the diagonal trace-zero space as $E$.
pitfall: The axial representation is det(R)R, not R on the full orthogonal group. Removing two polar vector rows gives the wrong internal symmetry under reflections.
prompt: Transform a rotation parameter across a reflection, then use all six edge constraints to identify the kernel.

edges: remove the three polar rigid modes
remove the three axial rigid modes

practice.question: When do polar and axial vector actions agree?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: For proper orthogonal transformations with determinant one. The axial action differs by det(R), which is one exactly on proper transformations.

practice.question: Under $R(x,y,z)=(x,z,y)$, how does the rotation parameter $(1,0,0)$ transform?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: To $(-1,0,0)$. The axial rule gives det(R)R times the parameter, and det(R) is minus one.

practice.question: Why are there no extra zero modes among symmetric strains?
practice.hint: Use the statement and the worked examples above.
practice.answer: The six paired edge equations force all off-diagonal entries and all diagonal pair sums to vanish. The explicit edge constraints prove injectivity on the six-dimensional symmetric strain space. Counts alone do not prove rank.

worked.title: Breathing from energy and from force
steps: For $S=qI$, all six edges extend by $q\ell_0$. Hence $V_2=6(k/2)q^2\ell_0^2=24ka^2q^2$. The kinetic energy is $(m/2)\sum_i\|\dot q r_i\|^2=6ma^2\dot q^2$.
The effective stiffness is $48ka^2$ and effective mass is $12ma^2$, so $\omega^2=4k/m$. Summing central spring forces at one vertex gives the same value, providing an independent factor check.

proofStatus: Complete proof for the stated model and hypotheses here
objective: Derive all internal mode shapes, exact frequencies, generalized masses and an independent breathing-force check.
